Debate resumes. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Van-ier (Mr. Gauthier) has the floor.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this debate shows once again that parliamentary democracy is strengthened when the House of Commons reaffirms its right to advise the government concerning appointments to important positions, such as officers of Parliament. We wish to protest such appointments today by requesting a debate on the appointment of the nominee for the position of Privacy Commissioner, Mr. Bruce Phillips.
Madam Speaker, we do so today with much regret, because the consultation which should have taken place, or which was indeed conducted was a one-way process. The government has indicated, at least to the Official Opposition, that it wanted to appoint Mr. Bruce Phillips. We said that the caucus which I represent might object to this appointment, and that it might be possible to negotiate or to arrive at a compromise. There was no mention of any leeway and, since the government did not
Routine Proceedings
wish to negotiate anything or consult on anything other than the appointment of Mr. Bruce Phillips, this debate is taking place. I think it is good, in a democracy, that the people of Canada should state their positions clearly and that in the case of such an important appointment as that of the Privacy Commissioner, a commissioner to protect the privacy of Canadians, Parliament should take time to reflect on the matter. In raising this issue, Madam Speaker, it is not in any way our intention to pass judgment on Mr. Bruce Phillips personally. We do not intend to question Mr. Phillips' integrity or honesty, nor his ability as a journalist, which he was for many years. We simply wish to remind the House of important elements to be considered by all when selecting a Privacy Commissioner.
When privacy is under attack, individual human dignity is under attack. That is why it is of the utmost importance that the members of this House should be able to discuss the appointment. As I said earlier, parliamentary democracy is strengthened when we can discuss in such an open and democratic manner.
We feel, Madam Speaker, that the role of the Privacy Commissioner, the public's perception of this role and of the person performing it, and the Commissioner's ability to act on behalf of all Canadians are most important and that is why we wish to raise objections to Mr. Bruce Phillips' appointment.
The Privacy Commissioner is appointed for seven years, as we all know, and he is empowered by the Privacy Act to receive complaints from Canadians and to investigate and report to the House on issues under his purview. He also reports regularly on the following five or six points: a refusal to provide personal information concerning an inmate in a federal institution; secondly, a request to correct or annotate a record of personal information, which is turned down by a federal institution, thirdly, when a federal institution has not provided within 30 to 60 days the personal information requested, the Privacy Commissioner can be asked to lodge an appeal.
Where the description of a record of personal information shown in the directory of personal information is not adequate, a correction can be requested.

June 7, 1990
Routine Proceedings
Where a federal institution has used personal information in a manner not provided for in the directory of personal information, one may seek correction and justice.
Finally, Madam Speaker, when a federal institution has not carried out the collection, conservation or retrieval of personal information concerning an individual in accordance with the act, the commissioner can again be asked to act on behalf of Canadians.
Therefore, not only has the commissioner the right to consult records held by the government, that is personal information records, he also has the responsibility of checking their content and, occasionally, of seeing that they are amended. The commissioner, Madam Speaker, is the ombudsman, the master and the defender of privacy in Canada. He is a most important person in a democracy, a person in whom we must all have total confidence.

Yesterday, the Minister of Justice shared her reasons with the House for the proposed appointment of Mr. Phillips. In doing so, she tried to draw a parallel between the outgoing commissioner, Dr. John Grace, and the proposed new commissioner, Mr. Bruce Phillips. I do not know Mr. Bruce Phillips. I have never met him in my life, but I might take this opportunity to reflect on the careers of both men, thereby establishing once and for all that comparing Dr. John Grace and Mr. Bruce Phillips is like comparing apples and oranges. It cannot be done.
Dr. John Grace has served as Privacy Commissioner for seven years. Previous to that, he served the CRTC as a public servant. Yes, he was a distinguished journalist. He was editor-in-chief of The Journal, a very respected newspaper in Ottawa that had to close down a few years ago because of reorganization of newspapers in Canada. Dr. Grace was the editor-in-chief of that paper, and it was not a Liberal paper. It was a well known Tory newspaper.
Mr. Grace did his job seriously and competently. For years, he was very involved in the community of Ottawa. He has our respect. He has proven over the last seven years as Privacy Commissioner that he could do the job well and in the interest of all Canadians. Therefore, he has our absolute confidence, and we will support the
nomination when the motion to appoint Dr. John Grace as Information Commissioner is brought forward.
We oppose the nomination of Mr. Phillips. Let us look at his career. From 1984 to 1987, he was the Minister of Public Affairs at the Canadian Embassy in Washington. He was there to filter information from the Government of Canada to the Americans. In 1987, he was brought to the front line of the Prime Minister's Office as Director of Communications for the Prime Minister. As we all know, he was responsible during 1988 for the message that went out from that office. Mr. Phillips was in charge of the PMO press office. He controlled the media's access to the Prime Minister. His partisan allegiance was well known.
It was quite evident to us that during the campaign Mr. Phillips was even in charge of what some newspapers alleged to be the dirty tricks campaign. He never denied The Globe and Mail articles we have and could read into the record which showed that Mr. Phillips was doing a job for the Prime Minister. We do not object to that.
Mr. Phillips was playing a political role. He was a competent journalist being put into a communications job to give Canadians the point of view of the Prime Minister. We do not object to that, but is it reasonable to ask Mr. Phillips to stand on guard today for Canadians on the privacy dossier and to stand up to the government which, in many cases, is the institution that is being questioned by Canadian individuals in regard to privacy?
Are we to buy, to approve or to rubber stamp the nomination of somebody who we know has been very partisan and who we know worked for the Prime Minister who surrounds himself with Tory hacks? We know that. Why should we accept that one of those go to a position of importance in Canada, Privacy Commissioner? He could be put into another job by Order in Council, even to the Senate if they want to. We would not mind that. Why not?
He would get $153 a day.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
He would get an additional $153 a day just for showing up.
We do not object to that, but we object strongly that Parliament, both Houses, the House of Commons and the Senate, be called upon to approve the nomination of a person who we all know is very partisan, who would have access to information on the opposition members of Parliament, into the privacy of every one of us. He will
June 7, 1990

be able to go into the records and see how we are doing. I do not want that. I do not think I can accept that.
I do not think he would be very objective in that regard. I do not think he could stand up here at the bar or anywhere else and defend the integrity of his impartiality in respect of opposition members, because he has over the years shown that he is not an impartial person. He is a very partisan individual.
That is all right. We do not mind that. We have some partisan people. I am a partisan individual, but I would not expect to be named Privacy Commissioner. I do not think the Tories over there would agree to that. They would certainly object, and I would agree.
How could you ever appoint anybody Governor General then?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
You do not do that by Order in Council. That is the problem.
There are many appointments here. I put the question to the Speaker on Monday of this week, asking what the difference is between an officer of the House and an officer of Parliament. There is no straight answer to that question.
I know that there are many, many positions. For example, the Auditor General, appointed by Order in Council. He answers to the House of Commons, not to the Senate. There is absolutely no way that you would agree that he is not working for Parliament. The Auditor General is a nomination of this House and of this House exclusively, not of Parliament. Yet he is responsible for public surveillance of the expenditures of the government.
It would not be appropriate to name the Minister of Finance to the position of Auditor General of Canada. I have a lot of respect for the Minister of Finance and his competence, even if I do not always agree with everything he does. I think it would be unacceptable to us if he was named Auditor General of Canada.
Needless to say, we have many articles in the press about Mr. Bruce Phillips' appointment. I will read an article here from Frank Howard on June 4, 1990. This is interesting. It states:
Routine Proceedings
Bruce Phillips has had so many different appearances over the last few years that it is asking too much from the public to accept this latest persona of probity, impartiality and conscience.
The sensitive nature of this post is such that we cannot have a reasonable doubt as to the probity, the impartiality and conscience of the Privacy Commissioner. There must be no doubt that he is absolutely above any reproach. We have hesitations and serious doubts.
I find the words of the outgoing Commissioner, John Grace, in his annual report of 1983-1984, interesting. He defines privacy as follows:
Privacy is not simply a precious and often irreplaceable human resource; respect for privacy is the acknowledgement of respect for human dignity and the individuality of man.
If nothing else, I would hope that all members of this House would want to provide this definition and apply this definition to the Privacy Commissioner. As I said, privacy is dignity. It is essentially what one has and once one has lost it, one has lost his dignity. We would like to reinforce the view that we would have somebody who has probity, impartiality and, of course, is perceived as being a person who will in all cases apply his judgment to these principles.
Madam Speaker, we are not the first to raise the question of the importance of the choice of a Privacy Commissioner. I could find you quotes from debates on access to information right from the start, in 1981-lots of quotes, from practically every member of the present cabinet, and here is one from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), when he was Leader of the Opposition, back in 1981, and he said, "Those who have the information have the real power".
In the case we are concerned with today, not only does the government have the information, a great deal of information, but into the bargain it is putting in charge of that information a person who was for a long time responsible for government propaganda. Now they are putting him in charge of information, which as we know is held by the government, sometimes to the detriment of Canadians.
Madam Speaker, at a time when Canadians' confidence in their government is at its lowest ever, I have trouble understanding how the government can persist in an appointment like this one. What Canada needs, Madam Speaker, is a watchdog, not a lapdog! We want

June 7, 1990
Routine Proceedings
someone in this position who will do a job that all Canadians can approve. And given that the Office of the Privacy Commissioner is an administrative tribunal-because in a sense that is what it is-it must be, and be seen to be, objective and absolutely impartial.
Madam Speaker, I could cite you quotes from Professor Patrice Garant, who in his Precis de droit des administrations publiques (summary of the law on public administration) says, "In our constitutional tradition, the quasi-judicial act is in the same category as the judicial act, and it must issue from a body protected from any political control or interference, as our courts of justice are."
The test, Madam Speaker, is this: should this position be protected from any government interference? We believe so, very strongly. The people of Canada must not feel that the government has any influence or might bring any pressure to bear on the Commissioner's office. This rule is all the more important for the administrative tribunals that make decisions affecting the public at large. For example, as far as the positions of Privacy Commissioner and Information Commissioner are concerned, we want them to be seen as totally and absolutely separate from this or any other government.
[English}
It has to be at arm's length. It has to be so far out there that they cannot touch him. He must be seen to be and perceived by Canadians to be totally independent of government. That is going to be very difficult for Mr. Phillips to do. It will be very difficult for him to meet the criteria that I just put.
I cannot see why he would want to, unless he has got something that I do not understand. How can he wash, clean up, and possibly eliminate his reputation of the last six or seven years as a Tory hack in charge of certain programs. We do not object to that. We have Liberal hacks too.
Quite an admission.
There is no such thing.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I will end this short expose, Madam Speaker, by saying that we would like this debate to come to an end. We know there is an agreement. We have agreed that we will vote on this. This caucus will vote against the nomination of Mr. Phillips, with regret.
I would like to end with one last comment. Frank Howard, in his article of June 4, 1990 in The Ottawa Citizen, said: "The person who is put forward as the candidate for the privacy job should look like he or she could stand up to the government of the day, not like somebody who is being rewarded for loyalty to the Prime Minister".

Madam speaker, I would like to put a few questions to the hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier.
Mr. Phillips, who is going to be appointed by the government to the position of Privacy Commissioner, has a responsibility which is extremely important. As the person in charge of the government's propaganda during the last federal election, it seems to me that he is in no position to have a sound opinion on what ought to be protected and what information ought to be made available to the public.
As you know, confidential Cabinet documents are protected for at least 20 years. In 1987 a recommendation was made by the Standing Commitee on Justice and the Solicitor General, on which I had the honour of sitting at the time. Our recommendation at that time dealt with the question of reducing the period during which more or less important documents, such as draft bills, for example, should be available to the public.
How can draft bills, which have to be debated by Parliament, be subject to confidentiality until they are tabled in the House? How can we as MPs discuss draft bills if they are kept confidential?
June 7, 1990

Mr. Phillips will certainly have every inclination to keep all these bills, all these documents, secret. I do not think he will be able to make a valid recommendation to the House once he has been appointed, because he will want to protect the government.
I would like to put this question to the Honourable member for his comment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I covered that aspect of the Honourable Member's question in my opening remarks when I said that we in the Official Opposition were not satisfied with Mr. Bruce Phillips' impartiality.
On the basis of the perception we have of this individual, even if we do not know him, but the perception of the information available to us, the perception of having seen Mr. Phillips act for the Prime Minister for seven or eight months, as information officer in Washington, or here in the Prime Minister's office during the last election, we all, including the hon. Member, know that Mr. Bruce Phillips, during the 1988 federal election used his position to tell the media what we say were untruths about the conduct and relationships of the Leader of the Opposition, to destroy in many cases his credibility-it was his job, but he destroyed the credibility of our leader, the hon member for Vancouver Quadra.

I have a quote that I would like to put on the record. It is from the first annual report of John Grace, the present Commissioner of Privacy, and it states: "Unlike trees or oil, information can indeed be renewed. Better computers linked to better communications systems can renew and expand information almost to infinity. But human privacy is not renewable, once lost to an indiscreet computer, a person's privacy is gone forever. The computer never forgets".
We are into an era of computerized information access. I, for one, am very nervous about naming a person who would have access to all government information when I know that he is less than objective in regard to his political affiliation.
Routine Proceedings

Madam Speaker, I think this could be a interesting debate for my colleague, because the man who has just spoken is certainly, among all the MPs, one of my best friends. So I shall try, while making one small comment, not to disagree wih him too much.
But during my political career, which after all has lasted some time, and even before as a student, I have observed this phenomenon. I have studied and observed this phenomenon which is still referred to as political partisanship. I have seen in Canada, for example, Supreme Court Justices who had been very partisan politicians, and yet who became great Supreme Court Justices. The question about Mr. Phillips, since it does seem that he will be appointed-I do not know at this time how I shall vote-but I do know what will be expected of him once he has been appointed to such a sensitive position, such an important position, and that is that he should be aware that he enjoys the protection of the House of Commons. He will not only have to be extremely prudent, but he will also have to renounce all political partisanship as we have seen in the past when certain individuals were appointed to high positions, such as the Bench.
And it is of the utmost importance for appointees to the Bench to know that they are fully protected by the law precisely to make sure that they are no longer political partisans. I find it unfortunate, since one may dream- and when I look at my colleague for Ottawa- Vanier, I like to think that maybe someday, if I had been the Prime Minister, he might have been-and I look at him as he is otherwise occupied-but if there is anyone that I would recommend as Commissioner of Official Languages, for instance, he is the one. Everybody will say no, he is a political partisan! Yet, if there ever was a man who is competent and qualified for this position-
Senator- Hear, hear!

The member is getting excited again.
Indeed, I wish to make an early announcement to the effect that if ever this position were to become vacant

and if he were to decide to end his political career, I would certainly agree to sponsor my honourable friend from Ottawa-Vanier-
Hear, hear!

As you can see, you already enjoy the support of all political parties, and yet my friend is very well-known in that regard.
In a nutshell, then, I repeat that this gives us an opportunity for which I thank you, Madam Speaker, to reflect once again as parliamentarians on the true meaning of political partisanship and to inform the people we appoint to such sensitive positions. And in that regard I agree with my colleague that we should make sure, since it does seem that Mr. Phillips will be appointed- I know him, he is a friend of mine, I am neither afraid nor ashamed to say so, I have known him for a long time. But I want to be certain that he understands the message of the House, which has been voiced by many members, not by myself, but by my esteemed colleague; now that it seems he will be appointed to this sensitive position, he will have not only to renounce all political partisanship but also to be seen as having done so. Very briefly, Madam Speaker, my colleague from Saint-Denis obviously still has a knack for comparing the incomparable. When you compare a judge with an officer of Parliament, I think there is still a difference. He is a lawyer. He knows there is a great difference between a Supreme Court Justice and an officer of Parliament, since one is appointed for seven years while the other is appointed for life. There is a time limit, and there is also a limit to the duties of those two persons. Such a comparison may appear valid to the Member, but I do not find it acceptable.
As concerns Mr. Phillips' purification, once he has been appointed-because the fact is that the government has a majority and will likely carry the vote-I shall be the first to applaud if he does. But he has a lot, really a lot of purification to do, Madam Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am a reluctant participant in this debate. In my view, this is a debate that ought not to be happening in the House.
I do not claim to have been here a long time, by any means, but it is the first time I can recall that an appointment by resolution of the House of Commons has had to be debated in the House. Normally, the subject of these appointments is by all-party agreement. Instead, we have this jackboot tactic from the government in proceeding unilaterally to impose its will on the House and the people of Canada in appointing someone who is a Tory hack to a position as an officer of Parliament. It is a disgraceful way to proceed. It is contrary to all the precedents. It is contrary to all past practice.
The normal procedure in making appointments to parliamentary posts is to consult with all the other parties and agree. In this case, it was obvious there was no agreement. In spite of that, this pig-headed government is proceeding with this resolution in the House.
As I say, I am reluctant to debate this kind of resolution, but I feel it is incumbent upon those of us who object to this appointment to make clear our reasons for so doing.
I have heard the hon. member for York Centre and the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier make very useful contributions to the discussion. I am not going to repeat all their remarks, but I will say at the outset that we on this side, as the others have said, have no dispute whatever with the distinguished career in journalism that Mr. Phillips brings to this job. In our view, that is not the issue.
I know some members may have reservations about columns that he has written or disagree with things he has said on the air, or whatever he may have done. That may be so. But we accept that that is part of journalism, that is the way it works, even though we do not always agree.
If the government had come forward with someone like Mr. Jeffrey Simpson, who is also a distinguished journalist as a nominee for this post, we would not object. But I would say right off that he writes columns that look like pamphlets for the next Tory campaign and he has been doing that for years. It is not the bias that we are concerned about in this case, it is the fact that this gentleman, Mr. Phillips, occupied a post in the Prime
June 7, 1990

Minister's office that necessarily involved him in highly partisan activities.
As I said before, I would have no objection to someone like Mr. Simpson, who writes for a Conservative newspaper, one that has become a sort of phoenix of the Ottawa Journal, which was one of the most Tory papers you could ever find in Canada. It was dreadful reading from our perspective. You could hardly find a picture of a Liberal in the paper; it was a dreadful thing.
The Globe and Mail seems to have taken over that role now and writes this apology for the government constantly, trying to justify the government's ill-conceived policies. Mr. Simpson writes these columns, as I say, that could easily be used as pamphlets for Conservative candidates in the next campaign, and my hon. friend from Halifax says they probably will be.
I am not going to argue that the gentleman is disqualified on the basis of partisanship. It is the fact that he has occupied a post that is beyond journalism, that in fact he was working in the Prime Minister's office as a party hack, as my hon. friend for Willowdale puts it so eloquently.
Yesterday in her speech, trying to justify this ridiculous appointment, this travesty, this outrage on the Canadian people, the Minister of Justice made some points that I want to deal with.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: The outrage is that you have the guts to stand up and say this.
The hon. member for St. John's East might listen. He might want to vote against this appointment at the appropriate time.
Yes, he might, but it is not likely.
I hope they are going to have a free vote on this issue in the House. I think we would find out what the Conservative back-benchers really think of this appointment.
Since free trade, you will never get anything free.

The Minister of Justice said, "If we are to say that any professional journalist who takes that job is thereafter tainted and cannot-take some other posi-
Routine Proceedings
tion without being tainted-that has very, very negative implications for the ability of governments to have the highest quality people serving them".
Is that fact, Madam Speaker? I say it is not. That is nonsense. The government can have Mr. Phillips serving it in any capacity it wants, and I stress the word "government". What we are talking about in this appointment is Parliament and Parliament is not the government. Parliament is not just the government; it is more than the government. Parliament is all the members of this House; it is all parties in this House. It is supposed to be the representative of the aspirations of all the people, not just the governing party.
The government is saying, "We would like Mr. Phillips to serve us as a government worker doing the job in Parliament". In other words, instead of representing all the people, it is putting him in as a government appointee as though this were a government job.
They could name him deputy minister. Maybe the Minister of Justice would like to have him as her deputy minister. She can make him that and we will not be in a position to stop it. The Minister of State for Finance might want to have him as his deputy minister. Fine. They might want to appoint him as head of the CRTC. They might want to make him chairman of any board or commission. There are lots of jobs and they are all full of Tory hacks. But they choose not to. They want to put him in a parliamentary job instead. That is what we on this side object to and our objection is one that is fundamental and it is fair. The minister also stated: "Therefore it is incumbent on those who wish to impugn Mr. Phillips' ability to provide some kind of evidence that he is not able to act with independence". What nerve the minister has in making that statement.
First, we have no obligation whatever to provide any evidence that he is not able to act with independence. That is not our job. Second, we are not impugning his ability. We are impugning his capacity-and there is a difference-to do this job. This is a quasi-judicial position. This position involves exercise of judgment, discretion, and exercise of considerable decision-making power over other people. The incumbent in this position must be seen to be acting impartially. Mr. Phillips will

June 7, 1990
Routine Proceedings
not be seen to be acting impartially. He will be seen to be acting as a party hack.
Third, the minister stated: "I would point out that in the period of time that he has been Assistant Privacy Commissioner, he has participated in putting together the report on drug testing that is veiy critical of the government". She seemed to suggest that because he had been critical once, we could assume that he would be critical whenever it was necessary. That is not evidence of impartiality. I am surprised that the Minister of Justice, as a lawyer, would even suggest that it was such evidence, yet that seems to be what she is putting forward. It is the only evidence that she has got.
The other tactic that the government has tried to use in this case came from the Minister for International Trade. I am glad he is here because perhaps he will want to bellow again. On Tuesday during Question Period he had quite a lot to say when very proper questions were being put by the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway was trying to ascertain certain facts about this dreadful appointment and the Minister for International Trade sort of exploded. There is no other word to describe it. He started to bellow from his seat and this is what he yelled, as recorded on page 12291 of Hansard:
What about Broadbent? What about the rest of you socialist horde?
I know he was not addressing our party.
What about what's his name, Lewis, who we appointed to the UN? What about that turkey? You don't protest about him. What about buddy down on the civil service board? What's his name? Ian Deans, what about him? That was all right. If Phillips was a socialist it would be all right.
It just shows the distorted thinking of the government ministers on this. I hope this is not a unanimous nomination. I hope it is just the Prime Minister, because if the other cabinet ministers agreed to this they have put their foot in it in a big bad way.
The fact is that these socialists were appointed to these positions and I am not, of course, agreeing necessarily with the words, the intemperate language used by the Minister for International Trade in describing some of the appointments. After all, he made the appointments. He and his cabinet made these appointments and they have to accept that responsibility. If they put turkeys into
the jobs, they cannot complain to us in the opposition about that. But there they are calling their own appointees turkeys. It was not very complimentary of the minister, I must say.
But the fact is these appointments are not to parliamentary jobs. These are government jobs. These are outside the purview of Parliament. They are appointed by the government by Order in Council. They do not come to this House and ask for a resolution of the House.
The Privacy Commissioner is different. The Auditor General is different. The Information Commissioner is different and the Chief Electoral Officer is different. Each of those posts are appointed by resolution of this House and then a subsequent Order in Council. If that is the way the appointments are done, then it seems to me there is an obligation on the government to come to this House and say we want all-party support for the appointment, not ramming some party hack down the throats of the Opposition. That is what is going on in this case.
For the Minister for International Trade to suggest that because they have appointed some socialists to government jobs, and I stress that, "government" sinecures, not parliamentary jobs and, therefore, somehow we should not criticize this appointment because this happens to be a Conservative, is rubbish. It has nothing to do with the issue that we are confronted with here which is whether or not Parliament is going to appoint some party hack to a position under the control of Parliament.
The Ottawa Citizen, which is hardly a newspaper said to favour the Liberal Party, has published today an editorial on this subject. I will only read part of it for the benefit of the hon member for St. John's East and perhaps the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader who I suspect too would want to vote against this appointment. It states:
The honourable men and women MPs of the Progressive
Conservative Party will carry out a dishonourable act today if they
approve Bruce Phillips as Canada's next Privacy Commissioner.
That is The Ottawa Citizen writing. They make it clear that the distinguished career that he has had as a journalist is not the problem. It is his close association with the Prime Minister's office that disqualifies him from an appointment to a parliamentary post.
June 7, 1990

The importance and independence of this position is evident from the fact that the appointment is to be made by Order in Council after resolution of both Houses. The appointment is for a seven-year term. This is not a short-term one or two-year appointment. This is a seven-year term and it is designed to ensure continuity in the job and independence in the appointee.
The government is dishonouring the post and this House in using its majority, if that is its intention and it is not going to declare a free vote on this issue, to thrash this unpopular nomination through this House of Commons.
I suggest that the appropriate course is for the government to withdraw this motion at once and come back and discuss it with the opposition parties-I know the New Democratic Party shares our view on this-and allow us to agree on an appointee worth putting into the job.
What the ministers have done is appoint people they are going to subsequently call turkeys, as the minister did the other day, and then try to say, look we have appointed these people, it is all right for us to go ahead with the others. We have allowed some of your people into jobs, so you have got to agree to ours.
That did not work with the New Democratic Party. They are still opposing this, in spite of the threats and bullying tactics of the Minister for International Trade. They cannot use that argument on us because they have not appointed the good Liberals to the jobs that they might go to.
I have one point of disagreement with the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier. I do not believe there are Liberal hacks. There is no such thing in the definition book, and the Minister for International Trade knows that and I think that he would agree with me on that point.
In conclusion, I urge the government to withdraw this motion at once and allow us to discuss the matter of this appointment in the usual way and come to an agreement. We are not disagreeable, but we have been given no alternatives. This was the only name put forward and I believe that it is inappropriate.
Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International
Trade): Madam Speaker, I would like to make several comments and ask the hon. gentleman for his opinion. I do not know why there is all this emphasis on hacks. Hacks are essential to the political process, whatever a hack is. Our people who want to assist in public service
Routine Proceedings
are being denigrated, attacked and scorned by having appellations such as the name "hack" applied to them-
Like poor Ian Deans?

The person who I suggested was a turkey is somebody in public life and there are many turkeys in public life, as we all know, but I am now addressing myself to somebody who has been called a hack.
My experience with the person under discussion is that he is a person who did a first-class job when he was a public commentator. When he was in the communications field on television, he was a perceptive observer of the Canadian political scene and fair and impartial in his comments.
Does the fact that he accepted a government appointment and then worked for the Prime Minister have him categorized, after a lifetime in the communications and other businesses, as some kind of a hack who is not capable of performing the duties of the office that we are now discussing? The course of action of the present Official Opposition is deplorable in this instance.
It is hardly relevant, of course, that they appointed, during their years in office, all sorts of persons who came with the same kind of background who had served them briefly or otherwise, and with that experience they should not be up with hypocritical remarks like this today. It is difficult to understand. One can understand the NDP because hypocrisy is a part of their make-up and they really do not know when they are being hypocritical and when they are not. I want to ask the hon. gentlemen who just made these remarks whether he agrees that Bruce Phillips is an outstanding person with a long background in public life, well able to understand and to enforce rights such as those he will have to enforce or comment upon during the next seven years that he would be in office, and that he is therefore a fine and suitable person for this office.
In ending, I want to put this piece of poetry forward for the consideration of the House.
Why take the track of Colleen Hack?
Why don't they just go quack, quack, quack?
All that is happening is just the fact
This action follows their well-laid track.
The NDP as ever, quake and shake
With indignation completely fake.
They never quivered, shivered or shook
When Ian Deans was given the hook.
The Public Service labour boards
Only wanted the NDP hordes
Appointed to important posts
By we PC governmental hosts.

June 7, 1990
Routine Proceedings
Gratitude not an NDP virtue.
Forgotten now are Broadbent and Lewis,
Still going forward to put screws to us.
Oh, oh!
Madam Speaker, I will not attempt to emulate the minister's poetic skills.
You are not from Newfoundland.

I am not from Newfoundland, that is true, but that is not the only reason I would not sink to emulate the hon. member's poetic skills. He reminds me of the great poet, McGonigal with his doggerel-I think it would be properly referred to.
To answer his question, no, I do not agree. I think he knows the answer to the question. He was simply taking advantage of the question and comment period to huff and puff a little. I am surprised, frankly, he did not apologize for his intemperate remarks that I quoted on Tuesday, insulting as they were, to the appointees that his government put forward. It was not the Liberal government that appointed these socialists to these posts. It was a Conservative government. It was not our responsibility to pass judgment on the quality of those appointments. They were done by the government on its own.
I want to say that we do not agree that this is a good appointment. I do agree with the minister when he says that Mr. Phillips is a very distinguished and competent journalist. That we have stated throughout and I do not think any member on this side has suggested otherwise. What I do say is that his past work in the Prime Minister's office disqualifies him from taking a job as an employee of Parliament. I stress that. The minister keeps missing that distinction. If he wanted to have Mr. Phillips on the Human Rights Commission or some other judicial body, that is the government's sole concern. What we are dealing with here is an appointment by this House and that is not just the government, it is all parties in this House. Surely the minister understands that distinction and he should cease trying to blur it because all the ministers on that side can do is blur that distinction and say we are doing exactly as we would normally be doing with any other appointment.
The three he has named and the socialists they have appointed have been named to government jobs not appointed by Parliament by resolution in this House. There is an important distinction and the minister should bear it in mind.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. May I address a question to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands.
This government, as we all know, has taken patronage to a new art form. The public finally rebelled. Even the journalists brought this to the attention of Canadians because they could not stomach it anymore.
That is right.

So what did the government do? It appointed the three socialists to say: "Oh, we are non-partisan". Then they call these socialists turkeys. Are they saying that all of their other appointments are worse than turkeys because they tried to clean up their act by appointing turkeys? This is obviously what this government is attempting to do. It has finally admitted to Canadians that its appointments throughout that rampant run of patronage were worse than turkeys. Does this mean that the government is going to recall all those appointments, ask for their resignations and make sure that we get a clean barnyard at least?

Madam Speaker, the point taken by the hon. member for Willowdale is a very good point. I was tempted in my remarks to cover the wide range of patronage for which this government has become so famous. Really, its disgraceful record of appointments since it took office in 1984 has left any past record of any prior government in tatters. This has really been a shocking, shocking orgy of patronage and that from a Prime Minister who in a national debate in the election campaign in 1984 protested his outrage at the 10 or 12 or 21 or 22 appointments, whatever the numbers were, that the Liberal government made just before that election. For this government to suggest that the three socialist appointments make up for the complete outrage it has perpetrated on the Canadian public is ridiculous.
I agree with the hon. member for Willowdale when he says that the minister is really letting the cat out of the bag in calling these three appointments turkeys, because these were the three star appointments. Every time we
June 7, 1990

accuse the government of being biased in its appointment process, it points to these three as examples of how pure it is, how virtuous it is, how non-partisan it is in making appointments. Now we are told by the minister that these three are turkeys. One wonders what the others are. Perhaps, when the minister makes another contribution he could enlighten us on that subject, perhaps with another poem about some of the other appointees.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise on debate with respect to these motions. Before commencing my remarks and putting this in a bit of an historical context, I do want to just set the record straight with respect to any suggestion that any of the three very distinguished appointees, about which the Minister for International Trade was bellowing and braying in the Elouse when I questioned the Minister of Justice, could properly be described as turkeys. Surely, nothing could be further from the truth. These three individuals have served and continue to serve the country with great distinction. I know that the hon. minister would not want to associate himself in any way with the suggestion that these individuals might be fowl of any description.
I also want to express my shock and surprise at the comments of the member for Kingston and the Islands. I know that member was not a member of this House in 1984, as I was. I was here, as was the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace and the member for York Centre, and I remember well that incredible orgy of patronage in June 1984. I know the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace and others were embarrassed and humiliated by that. When the member for Kingston and the Islands stands up in his place and says that the Conservatives have taken patronage to a new art form and so on, they merely learned from the masters; of course, the masters being the former Liberal government that appointed every former hack and flack and carrier-on and bag-person and member of Parliament who was terrified of facing the electorate. It put them all into juicy positions of one sort or another. I do not think the Liberal Party of Canada has any lessons to teach anyone about the debasing of the political coinage in this country through patronage.
Let us look at the appointment that Parliament is being asked to deal with today, because this is a very
Routine Proceedings
serious question. The Minister for International Trade has made light of it. The Minister of Justice in her extraordinary defence of this appointment has come up with arguments that boggle the imagination. She suggests that the fact that the Information Commissioner, John Grace, is a good friend of the former Leader of the Opposition would somehow mean that it is okay to appoint Bruce Phillips as Privacy Commissioner. What an absurd leap of logic.
The reality is that by appointing Bruce Phillips to this position, Bruce Phillips who had a highly partisan political job in the office of the Prime Minister, the government and the Prime Minister in particular are degrading and debasing the office of Privacy Commissioner.
Some people might say: "What is so important about the office of Privacy Commissioner?" I think we have to look back at the history of this appointment. I had the honour of serving on the justice committee which passed the legislation on protection of privacy and access to information. I believe the member for Willowdale was in the House in those days as well. He did not get appointed from 1984 to 1988 to one of those positions that his colleagues were appointed to, but he was here during the debate on that important legislation.
An essential element of the legislation was that the individuals, the men and women who were appointed to these positions of Privacy Commissioner and Information Commissioner would not simply be named by the Prime Minister or by the Minister of Justice. They would be appointed following a resolution of the House of Commons. The clear understanding of the purpose for that appointment process was to ensure that those appointments met with broad approval in this House, and that they not be foisted upon the House and the country by a government seeking to pay off its political friends. That is what has happened in this case. It is a very generous pay-off, I might add.
The Privacy Commissioner is a seven-year appointment with a salary of about $140,000. It is a nice way for Bruce Phillips to end a career in the Public Service. The pension is very generous indeed. But today, the purpose of dealing with this motion is to express our anger and sense of betrayal that the government would abuse the

June 7, 1990
Routine Proceedings
powers that it has in terms of numbers in this House to railroad this appointment through Parliament.
I want to point out that the threats to privacy in Canada are very real. In fact, in the most recent annual report of the Privacy Commissioner, John Grace, who has been moved to Information Commissioner, said just a couple of weeks ago: "The exponential growth of public and private data bases risks open season on Canadians' personal information".
"The last decade of the century," Grace said, "represents a rapidly closing window of opportunity, if the dignity of individuals is to be rescued from the voracious jaws of uncontrolled information and biotechnologies."
Who has the Government of Canada decided to appoint in this last decade of the 20th century to protect the privacy of Canadians? Who has it chosen to appoint to challenge the Prime Minister when he attempts to attack the privacy rights of Canadians? Why has it chosen to appoint a former officer from the Office of the Prime Minister, a former hack, a former political crony of the Prime Minister?
No one is questioning the credentials of Bruce Phillips as a journalist. That is not the issue. What we are saying is that in this appointment perception is as important as reality, and that the perception of those Canadians who are deeply concerned about the protection of their privacy against attacks by the government and the erosion of their privacy, is that a person who comes out of the Prime Minister's Office and goes into that position is not going to effectively stand up and defend his or her privacy.
This is not just any position. This was not a low level appointee in the Office of the Prime Minister. Bruce Phillips was the Director of Communications in the Office of the Prime Minister. He played a very active partisan role during the 1980 election campaign. In fact, Bruce Phillips admitted that during that campaign he called a lot of reporters and did whatever he could to attempt to get them to write articles and columns that were critical, such as hatchet jobs on John Turner.
That was the role that was played by Bruce Phillips who is now being proposed by this government as the guardian of privacy against the Prime Minister and against the Conservative government. It is unbelievable
that the government would actually appoint a person with that kind of partisan, political background in the Office of the Prime Minister to such a position. As the member for Kingston and the Islands has pointed out, this position is an officer of Parliament.
Politicians can stand in their places and be critical of this appointment, but I think the most effective criticism of this appointment comes from a very distinguished professor who has been acknowledged as an internationally respected expert on privacy. I am speaking, of course, of the very distinguished professor from the University of Western Ontario, David Flaherty.
I will quote what John Grace had to say about David Flaherty in his annual report:
Professor David Flaherty of the University of Western Ontario is an internationally recognized authority on data protection. He served as consultant to the Justice and Solicitor General Committee's review of the Privacy Act and he has been reported before in (reports of the Privacy Commissioner).
He has written one of the internationally respected texts on privacy called Protecting Privacy in Surveillance Societies.
What does Professor David Flaherty have to say about the appointment of Bruce Phillips, the Prime Minister's buddy, to this position of Privacy Commissioner? Professor David Flaherty said that he was disgusted by this appointment. Professor Flaherty, by the way, is certainly no socialist. I understand he may even be a red Tory. His credentials in the area of privacy are recognized throughout the world. He may be as red a Toiy as the member for Rosedale. I am not sure if that is possible, but he certainly is a respected privacy expert. He said that he was disgusted by the appointment. He went on to say that this appointment of Bruce Phillips ruins the integrity of the Office of Privacy Commissioner.
I would have hoped that hearing those words from this respected professor, this international expert on privacy law, the Minister of Justice might come back into this House and say: "Yes, I have made a mistake. The Prime Minister made me do it; the Prime Minister forced me to do it. I had no choice, but I am not going to carry through on this appointment. I respect the fact that Professor Flaherty and others have said that this is an unacceptable appointment".
Even the hon. member for St. John's East, I know, is cringing in embarrassment at this appointment. I would
June 7, 1990

have hoped that perhaps the Minister of Justice might come back and say: "Okay, I am prepared to withdraw the appointment". Or, at the very least she could accept the reasonable suggestion that has been made on a non-partisan basis that this appointment be referred to a parliamentary committee.
The Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General or another committee would then have an opportunity to call witnesses, for example Professor Flaherty or Ken Reuben, another very respected commentator in the field of privacy law, who has also expressed deep concerns about the appointment of Bruce Phillips. The committee could call Bruce Phillips himself before the committee and ask him just what it is in his experience in the Prime Minister's Office that qualifies him for this very important position.
I cannot over-emphasize the significance of this position in Canada today, the position of Privacy Commissioner. One has only to read the most recent annual report of the Privacy Commissioner to know the range of issues which are dealt with. We know that the Privacy Commissioner has tabled a number of important reports in the area of random testing for drugs, for example, and the whole area of AIDS and the importance of dealing sensitively and compassionately with privacy concerns in the area of AIDS.
We also know that there will be occasions when the Privacy Commissioner will be called upon to challenge directly the Office of the Prime Minister. We know and we remember all too well the fact that the Information Commissioner Inger Hansen has issued a number of very serious criticisms of the role that the Prime Minister's Office played in attempting to screen and vet information which was released to the public.
I might just say on that point that the treatment of Inger Hansen, an outstanding public servant, a woman who has contributed a great deal to this country as Information Commissioner, in her previous capacity as Privacy Commissioner and as the corrections ombudsperson has been shabby and beneath contempt. To treat a woman of this calibre and with this kind of distinguished record of service to her country in the way that this government has treated her is absolutely unbelievable.
Routine Proceedings
We know that she has been critical of the government. In fact in a number of speeches she has been particularly harsh in her criticism of this government's failure to move forward in respect of openness and accountability in government. In 1988 she said: "Investigations often reveal a picture of a government that uses every opportunity to say no or, if that fails, to delay the process."
In September 1988 she said: "With few exceptions, there is no longer any clear message from the government, whether from the politicians or the bureaucracy, that Canadians have a legislated right to access and that the law ought to be obeyed in a willing, forthright and timely fashion."
Inger Hansen spoke out independently, not always perhaps as strongly as some of us might have liked, but she spoke out independently and was prepared to take on the government.
The concern of Canadians is that the appointment of Bruce Phillips signals that instead of putting into place a strong and effective watch dog for the privacy of Canadians, we are getting a docile lap dog that will do what the Prime Minister's Office wants and will not challenge in any effective way decisions which are made by that office.
The debate today gives us an opportunity to voice our concern about this abuse of the appointment power of the Prime Minister to put into this sensitive and important office one of his former political colleagues. I would hope that this House might take the opportunity, when this comes to a vote as indeed it will, to issue a stern rebuke to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Justice to tell them that this position, which after all is an appointment of Parliament, is too important to debase by appointing an individual who was a political crony of the Prime Minister.
I would hope that members of this House would recognize that we can send a clear message to our constituents and to all Canadians that we believe strongly in the protection of the privacy of Canadians. The most effective way of doing that is by putting into this important office an individual who is seen to be independent, strong, effective, and not in any way tied to the Prime Minister's Office or to the government of the day.

June 7, 1990
Routine Proceedings
Bruce Phillips does not meet those criteria; in fact quite the opposite. It is for that reason that I am rising in my place to oppose this appointment, to urge the government to withdraw this appointment, and to urge all members of this House to show their disgust and their revulsion at the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice in their decision to politicize this appointment by voting against it when the opportunity comes in a few minutes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hesitate to enter this debate, but I have been drawn into it by both my friend here from Burnaby-Kingsway and my friend from Kingston and the Islands.
Perhaps I am in a unique position in this House, having been a political hack myself for a number of years, having worked with Mr. Phillips in the Prime Minister's Office, and having had to deal with Mr. Phillips supposedly as a Tory journalist. He was a most difficult, terribly unco-operative person. I can remember the 1979 budget when all we asked was that they not go until the Minister of Finance had read his speech. This Tory laughed me out of his office.
This man was a journalist, a respected journalist in this city and across this country. When he was asked to serve his country in our embassy in Washington, one of our most important embassies, he decided to do it not unlike a number of other people who have done exactly the same thing. Like a number of public servants and others, he then accepted an appointment in the service of the Prime Minister of this country.
There is no question, absolutely no question that one assumes some political responsibility, but as in many cases people return to the Public Service.
Having been a hack, a word I have used myself, I absolutely resent the concept and thesis that one cannot continue to serve one's country after a political life whether in the service of Parliament or in the service of the government. Whatever party we are from now or in the future I resent that we are all absolutely tainted with partisanship. It is offensive to me and to everyone else who served in the political system for whatever party he or she is in.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member may attempt to make up in volume what he lacks in substance to his argument.
The reality is that the hon. member for St. John's East who is generally a thoughtful and learned member of the House has fundamentally missed the point in this instance. No one is suggesting that Bruce Phillips has disqualified himself from continuing to serve in a whole range of other occupations.
However, what is being suggested in this instance is that because the Privacy Commissioner is an officer of Parliament and because that position must be recognized as being fundamentally independent of any attachment whatsoever whether past, present, or future to the Office of the Prime Minister, it is a fundamentally different situation.
As the hon. member for St. John's East has indicated, Bruce Phillips has served his Prime Minister with distinction. Indeed he played a very vigorous role during the federal election campaign. That is fair ball. He has served his country in our embassy in Washington, but this office is an office that reports directly to Parliament. It is an office that is charged with the responsibility of protecting the privacy of Canadians from ever encroaching demands on their privacy. For that reason it is essential that there not be the slightest suggestion that the holder of that office have any tie whatsoever with the Office of the Prime Minister.
It is like the hon. member for St. John's East. After the next federal election he will be looking for a job. No one would suggest that he should not be in a position of serving his country in a variety of capacities, given his lengthy service to the public. I am sure that Prime Minister McLaughlin will keep that in mind.
What must be understood clearly is that if there were any suggestion at the end of the term of Bruce Phillips that the hon. member for St. John's East were to be appointed to that position despite his very strong and distinguished credentials, it would be seen as unacceptable. I doubt whether he would suggest that somehow his experience in the Prime Minister's Office or as a member of the House, albeit for one term, would qualify him for that position.
As Professor Flaherty has said-I remind the House that he is not a politician- this appointment ruins the integrity of the office of Privacy Commissioner. It is not because Bruce Phillips has in the past served his country. It is because of the fact that he is being appointed to this office that this appointment is fundamentally unaccept-
June 7, 1990

able to not only us in the opposition but to all Canadians I am sure.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway on his speech and on his reasoned comments.
I must say that the hon. member for St. John's East is beginning to sound like his counterpart, the hon. member for St. John's West in his intemperate outbursts. My question for the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway will be more reasoned and sensible.
In the last few days, in fact most of this week, the New Democratic Party has been stressing the importance of the Senate under our Constitution. It has urged the Senate to exercise its constitutional right to stop government bills. I know this new-found interest in the Senate represents quite a change of heart because their policy had always been to urge the abolition of that chamber of sober second thought. We witnessed the spectacle of them having moved a motion on Monday, pointing out the Senate's powers, and last night voting against paying the Senate any of its money so they could continue to do their work. It was something of an amazing feat and gives some credence to the comments that the Minister for International Trade made earlier.
Leaving all that aside, I wonder if the New Democratic Party today is urging the Senate, when it considers its resolution in respect of this appointment to block this appointment. Is it part of the New Democratic Party policy to urge the Senate to stop this appointment by refusing to pass the counterpart of this resolution in the other place? I would be interested in the hon. member's views.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased that the member for Kingston and the Islands has given me an opportunity to voice the sense of outrage that Canadians from coast to coast are feeling about Liberal senators voting for themselves $153 a day just for showing up in the Senate.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, I know, is probably as embarrassed and as ashamed by the actions of his Liberal colleagues in the other place, at getting up and tottering to their seats and raising their
Routine Proceedings
hands and saying, "Yes, yes, I want $153 a day just for showing up". It is damned outrageous.
That is the position that Liberal senators, each and every one of them in the other place, have taken. It is shameful. I think Canadians from coast to coast are recoiling in revulsion at this spectacle of Liberal and Conservative senators. Liberal senators have the majority, and if the Liberal senators had the intestinal fortitude and the spine to stand up and say no, that they were not going to vote themselves $153 a day just for showing up, things might have been different.
When we talk about hyprocrisy, I suggest that the member for Kingston and the Islands and the member for Willowdale, go down the hall to the senate chamber and talk to the Liberals senators and beg and plead with them to reverse this decision to grant themselves $153 a day. Canadians are appalled by this kind of Liberal wallowing at the public trough.

Madam Speaker, I have listened to the unctuous outflow of words from the member for Burnaby-Kingsway. My hon. colleague for Kingston and the Islands asked him a very simple question, a question that the member from Kingston and the Islands even felt that he might be able to understand.
He didn't answer it.

He was afraid to answer. It was a simple question. If, in all his outrage, he is prepared to say Canada does not deserve Bruce Phillips as our Privacy Commissioner, will he ask the Senate to scupper this appointment?
That's right, why won't he do it?
Why will he not come clean and confess that he is being a hypocrite on this issue?
He is waiting for Audrey.

What does he want? Is he waiting for instructions from his new leader? Does he only want to criticize the Senate, but not use it in an instructive way? Is he suggesting that the country should be burdened with the goods and services tax even if the Senate has a possibility of stopping this iniquitous tax from going through? Is this what he is saying? He would refuse to answer that question.
Let us return to the issue of Bruce Phillips as Privacy Commissioner. First we have to make the record very clear. On this side of the House, we believe that Mr. Phillips has been a distinguished Canadian journalist.

June 7, 1990
Routine Proceedings
Second, he has served with distinction his own party, the Tories. Third, because of point number two, he is disqualified from serving in any one of four posts.
Our position is that anyone who has served the government or any other party in such a partisan way, is disqualified from only four government appointments. One of those is the Auditor General, the person charged with overseeing on a non-partisan basis the expenditures of government.
The second office for which he would automatically be disqualified because of his past, is that of Chief Electoral Officer, again an appointment of Parliament, a servant of Parliament and not of the government.
The third position for which he would be disqualified to serve would be Information Commissioner, a person charged with ensuring that Parliament itself has access to all the relevant information.
The fourth position is the one to which this government is appointing him, the Privacy Commissioner, dealing with the rights to privacy of all Canadians and again, a servant not of the government, but of all Canadians through all members of Parliament.
We are saying there are only four positions that we feel a person in Mr. Phillips' position is not qualified to serve in. This is not to denigrate from the individual, but this appointment is taking to the height of partisanship what should be an appointment totally beyond reproach.
Let us look at this government's record of appointments. We remember before the 1980 election when there was a certain prominent Tory in this country who talked about the beauty of getting one's snout into the trough; another barnyard analogy taken to new heights by the member for St. John's West. There was also that statement when this particular leader of Canada was asked if he would ever appoint a Liberal to any government position, to any Order in Council appointment? The answer was: "Not as long as there is one living Tory".
We saw a spate of appointments which were an embarrassment even to the most partisan of Canadians. We saw the appointment of one person to the board of Air Canada. This person was asked about qualifications to serve on the board of Air Canada: "What do you know
about transportation?" The response was: "I drive a car".
Really! Profound!

This was the quintessential type of appointment that was made for so many years by this government. Finally, it was so revolting to even members of the Tory party that they smartened up. They started to make some non-partisan appointments so that they could say their hands were clean. They appointed three prominent NDPers, socialists, to high positions. I must say I do not criticize those appointments because I thought all three of those NDPers had served their country with great distinction before those appointments were made, and are doing so or have done so in the posts to which they were appointed.
Was it out of a genuine interest in filling these posts with distinguished Canadians that they appointed Mr. Lewis to the UN, Mr. Broadbent to his position, and Mr. Deans to the Public Service Commission? Was this out of a sense of wanting to fill these posts with the best people? That was not their motive, even though they might have inadvertently made fine appointments. Their motivation was to attempt to cleanse their bloody hands from the past record they achieved of taking patronage to an all-time art form.
An orgy of patronage.

An orgy of patronage, as the member for Kingston and the Islands says. This did not just bring only the Tory party into disrepute. I must say that I think it cast all politicians in a bad light. When one politician does not act with the best interest of Canada in mind, Canadians do not say that it is just another Tory stunt, I think all of us suffer and are diminished in the minds of Canadians.
As elected representatives of whatever political stripe become diminished, we lose the ability to lead Canadians. We lose our ability to encourage Canadians to pull together. We have critical roles to play in order to make Canada great. We must be united as Canadians. We must work together to tackle global markets, rather than fracturing and fighting among the provinces, among sectors and among regions. When we as politicians make this call for Canadians to act together, but some politicians have misbehaved, we have lost our credibility. This
June 7, 1990

is the tragedy of the Tory record of downgrading politics in Canada, through terrible appointments based strictly on patronage.
I am not saying that governments prior to when the Tories took over some six years ago always made appointments based totally on merit. However, when I look at appointments we made such as Gordon Fairweather, a prominent Conservative-
A cabinet minister.

-cabinet minister who Prime Minister Trudeau appointed to head up the Human Rights Commission. The fact that he was a Tory did not enter into the issue at all. There was a human being whose record on human rights, before he went into that post and before he was appointed, qualified him as the most pre-eminent Canadian to fill that post and Canadians rejoiced. They did not have to ask about his political stripe. It was an appointment of distinction and merit.
I can think of lots of examples where the same type of non-partisanship was followed; Mr. Duff Roblin, Ernest Manning, and Premier Smith to the Senate. These were appointments that brought distinction to the institution to which they were appointed. It brought distinction to the government that appointed them and it brought distinction to all politicians because we are all part of a process which was regarded as being higher than the levels to which this government has brought us through its grovelling in the trough of patronage.
Bruce Phillips is a journalist of distinction and a person who has served his party with distinction, albeit in a highly partisan way. We are saying that there are only four offices for which that individual cannot be qualified because of his former partisan activities; Auditor General, Chief Electoral Officer, Information Commissioner and the Privacy Commissioner. Every other government Order in Council appointment office would be open to this individual.
That does not mean we would not reserve the right to criticize an appointment were he not qualified to fulfil that task. We no longer want the qualifications for serving on the board of Air Canada to be the response: "Well, I know how to drive a car".
Routine Proceedings
Let us, as politicians from every side of the House, think about how our constituents, the people of Canada, look on us. What are the highest possible standards they can expect from us?

What would Canadians' reaction be if it could be said that this man or this woman was the best qualified for the position, the best qualified of any Canadian, with partisan considerations completely set aside, no importance given to his or her political affiliation? The government must, for the first time, become a leader. A leader that can set an example with its appointments to these very important posts. It would be very simple for the Prime Minister to say to Mr. Bruce Phillips, "I'm sorry, I made a mistake in asking you to take on this job. We have something else for you. But the Parliament of Canada must be safeguarded, it must be protected, and we must appoint people who have not previously been partisan." For four positions, that is all.

We are looking for leadership from the government. All it has to do, not only in order to win the respect of Parliament, but to give a new attitude to Canadians, is to say to Mr. Bruce Phillips: "I am sorry. This one post is not open to you. We will give you something else and then we will judge based on qualifications."
I think Canadians expect more of their government. They expect more of all politicians of whatever stripe. If we are going to start winning back their respect so that they will listen to us, is this not a marvellous opportunity, by a simple act, reversing a partisan appointment which is an abuse of Parliament? This can be done by reversing one simple nomination. Bruce Phillips does not have to suffer because of that, because he can be named to some other post for which he is better qualified. It is a simple act of reversing this one nomination, therefore restoring the integrity of this institution and restoring the faith-

-the faith of Canadians in our government, in our system of government, in the Parliament of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I would like to put two questions to my hon. colleague. I should start out by saying that I greatly appreciated his speech, his comments. My first question is this: I wonder if he remembers the debate in 1984 about this important issue, and the commitments Mr. Mulroney had made at the time. What was it that he supposedly intented to do? You will remember, I am sure, that he made some serious commitments. What

serious commitments. What bothers me is that I have the impression that his commitment in this important area, which affects the very soul of politics in Canada, seems to be just like all the other commitments-what is said and what is actually done are two different things. I would like you to elaborate on that.
My second question is the following:

Could the hon. member not only elaborate on the promise that was made during that debate, but perhaps say a few words about the record of the government in terms of what the commitment was then? I think that is rather important. In fact, I think it is critical and I think Canadians want to know what was said and what was done.

Madam Speaker, those are both good questions. The first related to what the Prime Minister said during the 1984 election campaign. He said two things to the people of Canada. He promised that there would never be any patronage, that his would be an open, an honest government.
He said a new era was opening up for Canadians as far as government appointments were concerned: appointees would be qualified people, experienced people, good people. That is what he said to Canadians.
But this is what he said to the Quebec Conservatives when he was asked if he would appoint a Liberal to any position-he said, "Yes, but not if there's even one Conservative still alive". So he said two things.
But what he did, as my hon. colleague from Manitoba has suggested, what he did after the election was something else entirely.

We saw exactly what happened. There was a spate of appointments and competent people who had served in posts with distinction were "unappointed". I will give you a very good example.
The Hon. Barney Danson, who had been our distinguished Minister of Defence, had been appointed to serve in a top post, representing Canadian business in Boston in the United States. It is not an incredibly important post in terms of the posts that are created, but the Hon. Barney Danson went to Boston with his wife and they created a whole new set of industries involving Canadian trade because he knew how to promote Canada. The Dansons worked hard at that post helping to put forward Canadian interests. What happened? A person with unquestioned competence, integrity, and ability did not get re-appointed so that the post could be filled by someone else.
There were so many appointments it started to gall Canadians. Every day the headlines read: "Another snout in the trough". Even Conservatives were embarrassed after 1984, through 1985 and 1986, by the appointments that were being made.
The hon. member, my esteemed colleague from Manitoba, points out that the appointments made after 1984 were not in accordance with the promise made to Canadians. However, perhaps we can give the Prime Minister the benefit of the doubt; they were precisely in accord with the promise he had made behind closed doors to Conservatives in Quebec.
What we have seen is an attempt by the government to clean up its act and its image by appointing some prominent NDPers to posts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: How would that clean up the act?

The hon. member from Halifax asks how that would clean up the act. The Prime Minister has cited those as being great appointments, but obviously the member from Halifax is disagreeing with his own leader. I have never seen such lese-majeste.
We have behind me here a member from Calgary who was kicked out of that caucus for a lesser disagreement and one of greater principle than what the member for Halifax West exclaimed right now.
If the member for Halifax West is saying that he disagrees completely with the appointment of the three socialists made by his Prime Minister, then I submit that, if he does not resign from the Tory caucus right now, it is greater cause for being drummed out of caucus than the member from Calgary sitting behind us on this side who resigned on principle simply because he refused to support the GST.
