Because he listened to the people.

The member for Halifax West might have a point, because the member for St. John's West earlier called these three appointments, which the Prime Minister has lauded and touted throughout Canada, the appointment of turkeys. I assume that the member for Halifax West and the member for St. John's West are in agreement that their Prime Minister was wrong in making these appointments. They are now publicly criticizing their own Prime Minister for having made these great appointments.
I would hope they would do the honourable thing and submit their letters of resignation to the Prime Minister. They could do a joint letter signed by Halifax West and St. John's West. They could say: "We do so because we disagree with your appointment of those three socialists to these posts, appointments that were made in an attempt to cleanse our image even though, before Canadians, our hands are still bloodied. Like Lady MacBeth, these hands the multitudinous seas would incarnadine."
I suspect they will be sending this letter to the Prime Minister, doing the honourable thing, because the Prime Minister tried to clean up his act by making some non-partisan appointments.
I suspect that the hon. members opposite are happy with this appointment of Bruce Phillips. I am talking about only two members, the member for St. John's West and the member for Halifax West. They must be happy with this appointment of Bruce Phillips because they feel that other appointments by the Prime Minister have been wrong, when he appointed socialists. Bruce Phillips is obviously not a socialist. He has been there in the troops with them, he has been there in the forces, and he has been in the trenches. He was manipulating the fifth estate on their behalf in order to give the spin that the Tories needed in order to bring home victoiy to them in 1984. He was doing it afterward and he has been good for them.
All we are saying is that Mr. Phillips, a distinguished journalist, a strong hack for the Tory Party, has disqualified himself, because of his previous partisan activities, only from serving in four posts which are parliamentary and not government.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to read a message which I received from the students of St. Boniface Diocesan High School. They met the day before yesterday in front of the legislative building in Manitoba to show their commitment to national unity.
I quote parts of this letter:
We, the undersigned, are proud of who, where and what we are. We are proud of Canada's unique identity as a friendly nation that extends from sea to sea, but more importantly, as a country capable of sustaining two separate cultures in relative harmony.
The present situation has brought, perhaps, the beginning of the end of our concept of Canada.
Those in Quebec have been exposed to some very inaccurate representations of English Canadian feelings towards French Canada. The media have shown isolated incidents involving antiFrench rallying and have continued to dwell on the negative. It is the purpose of this letter to show that positive feelings do exist and that we are very worried about the unity of our country.
They go on to give an example of the sharing of the school between St. Boniface Diocesan High School and Ecole Precieux Sang. The letter continues:
We are feeling that, perhaps, the people of Quebec do not realize just how much support they have in the west. To reinforce our confidence in the strength of Canada, we publicly proclaim our support of Quebec and a united Canada.

I ask all young Canadians throughout Canada to express their feelings right away on this extremely important issue and to show that they really want a strong united country.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend and congratulate the students of the grade 10 English class in Lockeport High School and their teacher, Cliff MacKay.
These students collectively wrote a play entitled "The Lockeport Story: Past, Present, and Future". It tells the story of their town and its difficulties in recent years with the trials and tribulations of the fishing industry. This play which was collectively written by the 24 students and their teacher was performed before over 300 people in three performances.
The play reflected the heart, the soul, and the character of the town of Lockeport, a town in which people recognize that they are the best ones to deal with and solve their own problems. The recent history of Lockeport has been one of trial but with the type of leadership and self-reliance demonstrated by these students of Lockeport, I am confident that the Lockeport story will have a happy ending very soon.

Mr. Speaker, analysts of Canada's airline industry are sounding warning bells. There is every chance that only one of our two major airlines will survive this decade.
New Democrats warned the government of this issue. Symptoms of serious illness in this industry are now undeniable. Air Canada posted a $13 million loss this year in its first quarter, for the second year running. It would have been even worse had it not sold off $21 million in assets.

June 7, 1990
Canadian Airlines is in no better shape and may well be doing worse with PWA haemorrhaging cash, 1,600 lay-offs since the Wardair purchase, and 1,900 more jobs slated for the axe in the near future.
The signs are there that soon there may be only one airline, and the government must be ready. That means preparing to protect consumers from monopoly price gouging and preparing to protect communities from service cuts.
I do not want to cry wolf, and perhaps some miracle may yet happen, but the government has a responsibility to Canadians to be prepared for a shrinking industry, especially when it helped to bring it about by deregulation.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to tell my fellow Canadians in Quebec-Est about a wonderful event that will take place in our riding on July 1.
Mr. Speaker, as part of Canada Day festivities, we will have the honour to celebrate the citizenship ceremony at the Franpois Charon Centre in Quebec City.
Since this rehabilitation centre symbolizes humanitari-anism, dedication and generosity in all respects, I think it is the ideal place to show our new Canadian citizens the spirit and determination that characterize our people.
Thanks go to the president and general manager, Louis Champoux, for the receptivity and eagerness he showed in granting this request. I look forward to attending this most important celebration soon.

Mr. Speaker, between 1914 and 1920, approximately 8,500 Ukrainian Canadians were interned in 26 concentration camps across Canada. Just because they came from an area of the world under
the Austro-Hungarian empire, they were used as forced labour in internment camps and had their property confiscated and never returned.
In October 1988, the Ukrainian Canadian Congress submitted a proposal to the Canadian government for the acknowledgement of and the symbolic redress for this injustice. This three-page proposal has taken over 18 months to study, and still this government is incapable of a response.
This is a legitimate concern and this government has the responsibility to respond. This is an issue about fundamental civil liberties, and it is important to all Canadians. This government must show a commitment to addressing these concerns by responding with action instead of silence.
Canadians must right a wrong. The federal government must right that wrong for them.

Mr. Speaker, there seems to be some misunderstanding, and I hope not purposely, by members of the New Democratic Party. They are saying that the Department of Health and Welfare has cut $4 million from the budget of the New Horizons Program.
I would like to take this opportunity to set the record straight. Fifteen million dollars was allocated to New Horizons projects in the main estimates. Of that, $4 million was temporarily set aside, not cancelled, pending a review of the program.
The purpose of the review is to see how the money could be better spent on projects within the New Horizons Program. As part of this review, senior citizens across the country will be consulted. I believe this is a positive step in ensuring that the taxpayers' money is spent on worth-while programs and that within those programs it is put to its best possible use.
This statement is made necessary in an attempt to negate the scare mongering that I attribute to those who use their information selectively.
June 7, 1990

Mr. Speaker, last week I asked a question of the Solicitor General on the issue of treatment of sex offenders, and he said that he was still studying the subject.
This week, a new book was published called Criminal Neglect: Why Sex Offenders Go Free. It is a horrifying account of the epidemic of sex offences and abuse in this country. I do not know whether the issue has always been around and is just becoming public, or whether there is a particular rise in the issue.
What is clearly documented here is the failure of society in general to respond to this problem, and the particular failure of Correctional Service Canada and the Government of Canada to deal effectively and fairly with the problem of sex offenders.
I urge the House and the public to take a look at this important book.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, this is Canadian Environment Week. I would like to pay tribute to Stora Forest Industries Limited of Port Hawkesbury, Nova Scotia for its bold initiative in environmental awareness.
Earlier this year Stora launched an environmental awareness program for all 1,000 of its employees, as well as more than 200 woodlands contractors and related personnel. The program, the first of its kind in the pulp and paper industry in Canada, enabled participants to educate themselves on global and local environmental issues, on forest management, and on what Stora as a pulp and newsprint producer was doing in the area. Through these workshops employees participated in the development of an environmental policy for the company.
On Monday I participated in this workshop, along with 21 other media, educators and community leaders. The session was engaging, informative, and frank. Stora admitted that it was not perfect but was honestly committed as a corporation to conducting its affairs consistent with the principles of sustainable development and of sharing its successes and failings openly with the wider community.
This is responsible corporate citizenry, and I urge industry across Canada to follow Stora's lead.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow morning at Rideau Hall His Excellency the Governor General will present bravery decorations to 13 Canadians for acts of heroism. The recipients have each demonstrated the strength and courage that we each like to have in times of trial.
One example of the unselfish heroism that will be recognized occurred last year north of Drumheller, Alberta. Eighteen-year old Derrick Wilson watched from the ground as his uncle Dale's crop dusting plane slammed into a field and burst into flames. Without apparent thought for his own safety, Derrick ran to the upside down plane, pulled his semi-conscious uncle free, and extinguished his burning clothing.
Derrick will be recognized with the Medal of Bravery but more important is the knowledge that his unselfish act saved his uncle's life. When interviewed by the media he was quoted as "not wanting to brag about it".
On behalf of this House, I would like to congratulate Derrick and the other 12 recipients of the bravery decorations. They are Canadians we can all be proud of.

Mr. Speaker, after some intense negotiating, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities managed to bring the GST for municipalities down from 7 per cent to 3 per cent.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said that the FCM had been very diligent and effective in its defence of the interests of municipalities, and that all parties had to show some flexibility in order to deal with a number of complex issues and obtain a satisfactory GST rebate for municipalities.

June 7, 1990
The government's goal, said the minister, was to ensure that after the sales tax reform was ratified, municipalities would not take up a heavier tax burden than the one they have now.
Mr. Speaker, we want to thank the Minister of Finance who made a major concession and reduced the GST to 3 per cent for Canadian and Quebec municipalities.

Mr. Speaker, on April 17, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans stated:
Fishermen need safe, accessible harbours as much as they need
serviceable vessels and gear.
The fishermen of my riding of Egmont and the other three ridings of P.E.I. would very much like the minister to translate his statement into action.
Across the island wharfs are collapsing because minimum maintenance has been neglected for several years. Fishing boats are running aground because harbours are being blocked by silt and dredging is not being carried out.
Many harbours are overcrowded because facilities which should have been expanded have actually diminished. Requests from fishermen have been ignored. Warnings from fishermen have been ignored. Fishermen's boats have been damaged and fishermen's lives have been put in jeopardy.
Fishermen of P.E.I. want this government to do its job: get the dredging done, get the wharfs repaired, and give the fishermen of Tignish, Alberton, Miminegash, Howards Cove, and Higgin's Wharf a chance to do their job and do it in safety.

Mr. Speaker, we all know that there exists those sceptics, those whose vision is short and whose aspirations are narrow who believe that Canada does not have a future united.
Do not believe these wistful dreamers. Let Canadians of good faith show by their actions that the vigour and the vitality of our nation is unimpaired, that our determination is to uphold the spirit of Canada, that our voice of
reason shall be heard in the councils of the world, and that we remain a strong, a vibrant, a modem and a generous nation, one which is accepting of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, how many toxic waste dumps are there in Canada? The government does not have a clue.
There is no complete inventory of toxic waste sites due to budget cuts in 1984. Across the nation there is a wide disparity in classification and even definition of toxic waste, so some provinces have become pollution havens with laws full of loopholes.
The rules and regulations for toxic waste under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act are gutless. Each province is held responsible under CEPA, but no equivalency agreements have been signed.
Why can this government not realize that strong national standards are the only effective way to clean up the environment? Today we have an unravelling patchwork of provincial regulations. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Members of this House will be interested to know that a former colleague of some of us and a former member of this place, Fred Stenson, died on June 5. Some members have requested the House to give tributes. I know the House would be in accordance with that. I call first the hon. member for Peterborough.
Tributes
June 7, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I rise to pay tribute today to the late Fred Stenson, who was a member of Parliament between 1962 and 1965. Fred represented the riding of Peterborough which I now have the honour to represent. Fred passed away this past Tuesday at the age of 75. His funeral service is being held today in Peterborough.
To my knowledge there are only two members left in the House today who were here when the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker was Prime Minister and when Fred Stenson was an MP. They are the member for Windsor West and the member for Saint-Denis. I am sure they both have very fond memories of Fred. I should also point out that the Hon. Stanley Knowles, now honorary clerk of the table, was also a member of the House during Mr. Stenson's term of office.
As reported in The Peterborough Examiner last night, Fred was often referred to as a doer. He was guided by the principle that instead of sitting around and talking about something, it is better to simply get up and do it. This philosophy was followed by Fred throughout his very distinguished career.
Prior to his election to Parliament in 1962, Fred served as trustee on the North Monaghan School Board. He then was elected to the North Monaghan Township Council for 10 years. He served as Reeve for four years and Deputy Reeve for two.
Fred Stenson was perhaps best known in the Peterborough area for his very successful farm. This love of the land remained with him after his election to the House where he maintained an acute interest in agricultural issues, working diligently to improve the plight of the farmers not only in his own constituency but in all parts of the country.
After his defeat in the election of 1965, a defeat that he took with distinction, Fred returned to his farm at which he worked tirelessly right up to the time of his death. It was also in this capacity, as an avid farmer, that you would see Fred every Saturday at the Peterborough Farmers' Market working at a very large fruit and vegetable stand. In fact, even last Saturday Fred was
there at his usual spot doing what he loved best, keeping in touch with the people and listening to their concerns.
It would be there at the Farmers' Market that I would often run into Fred. I would occasionally get his assessment of what he saw as the important issues in the region. This ability to fully understand the Peterborough area right from the grassroots level and up was what made Fred Stenson truly unique.
For myself, stepping into Fred's shoes some years later, it was these qualities that made him such an invaluable source of help and guidance to me. I will miss him a great deal.
To his wife Bernice, their children, Sally, Robert and Arthur, his sisters, Beryl, Muriel and Norma and all of their families, on behalf of myself and all members of this House, I extend our deep and sincere condolences.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very sorry to learn that Fred Stenson had passed away. I recall him as a serious concerned individual, a person who built on his previous career as a school trustee, as a member of township council, as a Reeve, to provide an example of serious, solid public service.
Fred Stenson provides an example of the kind of serious, solid public service which has helped to build so many of our communities and our country at large. This example should be important to all of us and, therefore, I am pleased to pay tribute at this time to Fred and to his memory.
I would like to express my deep and sincere sympathy to his wife, his children and his entire family. I hope that the memories of Fred and his contributions to family life and his community will help them surmount the sadness they face at his passing.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to pay tribute on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party to Mr. Fred Stenson.
While I was not a parliamentarian when Mr. Stenson served in a very distinguished way in this House, my friend and colleague, Mr. Stanley Knowles, the hon. clerk at the table, was.
Earlier today I spoke with Stanley about his recollections of Fred Stenson. Stanley remembers Fred as a respected colleague, a colleague who was admired by all and was a very likeable man. He was a grassroots
June 7, 1990

politician. Stanley described him as a person who spent a lot of time serving his constituents well and with distinction.
He was a hard worker. Mr. Knowles indicated that in committee work, in the House, in his constituency and about the country, he worked hard and spent time on a one-to-one basis with people, serving them in that capacity as opposed to speaking in the House of Commons at length.
He was an active man, involved in politics at the local level, indeed at the federal level. He was a realtor, service station operator and, above all, he was a farmer. In that capacity, Mr. Knowles and Mr. Stenson spent many hours discussing ways and means of assisting the farmer and the farm community during his time as a member of Parliament.
He was very active in his community. As the present member for Peterborough has indicated, only this past weekend Mr. Stenson was working in his stall in a Peterborough market. People over the years always knew him to be there serving his constituency and representing the community.
On behalf of a former colleague, Mr. Knowles, and the New Democratic Party, I say to Mrs. Stenson, his family and friends, our hearts and thoughts are with you today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: POSTAL AREA OF ORANGEDALE, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
I am
informed by Canada Post Corporation as follows:
a)	The revenues and operating costs of individual post offices are not made public by Canada Post Corporation.
b)	The value of contracts for retail postal outlets is based on actual work performed. Individual details are a private contractual relationship which are not disclosed by Canada Post Corporation. Remuneration is on a gross margin and fee-for-service basis.
c)	Canada Post discusses the service requirements and remuneration (as in (b) above) with interested businesses and evaluates all applications received. Canada Post does not negotiate between businesses with regard to remuneration. Service, security and credit considerations dictate the successful applicant. d)	The contractual arrangement between Canada Post Corporation and local businesses is a private business relationship and the values of such contracts are not made public.
e)	Rural route delivery is provided by a contractor. The value of this contract, as any other, is not made public.

The House resumed from Friday, February 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp that Bill C-44, An Act respecting the Hibernia Development Project and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Barrett (p. 8146).
Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International
TVade): Madam Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to have the opportunity to speak for a few minutes on the bill before the House today. It is a very important piece of legislation for the province of Newfoundland and Labrador and as a matter of fact for Atlantic Canada and for the country as a whole because it will have substantial economic benefits not just for eastern Canada but across the country, including the great province of Alberta and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec as well.
Of course the legislation deals with the Hibernia project. I believe in 1979 the consortium led by a Mobile Oil and the others who participate in it-Chevron, Gulf Canada and Petro-Canada- discovered oil off the east coast of the Avalon Peninsula in Newfoundland in what is known as the Hibernia fields. It is now 11 years later, Madam Speaker, so you can see how difficult it has been to resolve all the issues involved in bringing this oilfield into production. It has taken 11 years to get the project to this stage.
It is a massive project. It is a project that is taking place physically in an area-I have not had a chance to research all the statistics for this occasion because we have been busy in other directions-something like 170 miles off the shores of Newfoundland in an area that is frequently ice traversed, particularly during the winter and spring and where there are many problems to be faced and overcome in preparing to develop and take out the oil which lies beneath the surface of the land and sea in that particular area.
June 7, 1990

In 1985 there was finally a breakthrough with respect to jurisdiction over the offshore oil and gas resources that lay off Newfoundland and Labrador. That was a matter that was in dispute for a period of three or four years. It was settled by the government of which I am a member. I am veiy delighted and proud to have been a member and to be a member of the government that solved the conundrum and entered into an agreement with the province of Newfoundland and Labrador to provide for a fair way of managing this resource in which both the province and the Government of Canada would share.
That agreement known as the Atlantic Accord is being carried into effect by the legislation before the House today. From the summer of 1985 it took a further three years to July 1988 for all the detailed negotiations to be completed among the Government of Canada, the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, Mobil, and the Mobil consortium. The consortium that is going to develop and produce the oil of the Hibernia field is headed by Mobil Oil of Canada, and I think I have named the other parties involved in the consortium already. It took three years of hard negotiations to bring the project to the stage where all the issues were resolved with respect to agreement in principle. That was completed and announced in July 1988.
However, the completion of the final legal agreements necessary for this project took longer than expected. It was hoped it would be only a year, but rather than the project going forward in its final form in 1989, it is now our hope and our objective that the project will get its final approval in the summer of 1990.1 want to thank and congratulate the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his two predecessors for their work in bringing the project forward to this stage.
We have heard much in this House this year about the economic difficulties suffered by the people of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, particularly those who are connected with or associated with the fishery. We have heard considerable discussion both in this House and in the province of Newfoundland on the need for economic diversification in Newfoundland.
Government Orders
We have had an extensive regional development program in effect in Newfoundland for many years, including an accelerated program under the aegis of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency which has been operating for the last two or three years, and I think quite successfully.
However, it does not matter what financial assistance is made available, it is a very difficult matter to diversify economically the province beyond the natural resources of the province, its advantages of location or what have you. These resources in Newfoundland, the fishery, the minerals and the forests have been developed. What further are we going to diversify in? If there are problems in the fishery and we have to diversify so plant workers and those who are now fishing may have other economic opportunities, what are they going to be?
I have been in politics or public life for the last 25 years. My conclusion is this. There is no opportunity for any great economic diversification in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador that is not associated in some way with the sea; either what is in the sea, what goes on the sea, or what lies under the sea, as well as with our geographic location and the other natural resources that I have mentioned.
Our only major opportunity for economic diversification other than what already exists in Newfoundland lies with this offshore mineral potential, not just the Hibernia field but with the Terra Nova field and other fields that have already been identified and that will be developed once Hibernia is under way.
Since 1979, we have developed a number of high-tech industries in Newfoundland. These are companies which over the last several years have been just clinging on. Some are successful doing work in other parts of the world. There is a whole series of high-tech companies and persons now in Newfoundland, particularly located in eastern Newfoundland, who are ready to exploit the opportunities of the offshore once Hibernia starts and they are very anxious to see this project going forward.
I am very pleased to support this bill because I think that anyone who appreciates the need for economic diversification or other economic alternatives for the working man and woman of Newfoundland and Labra-

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
dor will realize that this is the only real alternative that presents itself.
This is a project that is receiving veiy considerable economic assistance from the Government of Canada. If Newfoundland was not part of the great Dominion of Canada, as it used to be called, I do not know where the necessary assistance would come from to see that this project was developed. I think that is something the people of Newfoundland and Labrador might well keep in mind at the present time.
I have not had a chance to refresh my memory today as to all of the means of assistance of the Government of Canada on this project, but I believe that our basic assistance is $2.7 billion which the Government of Canada is providing by way of grant or by way of guarantees of loans for this project. While I cannot guarantee these figures, the Hibernia project itself is going to require a cost, roughly, before it comes into production, of $5.1 billion.
So the investors in this project are going to have to put in $5.1 billion before they have an opportunity to receive one cent of return on their investment. The total capital investment will be $8.6 billion before the Hibernia field is completely developed and the oil removed. The operating costs during that same period will be another $12 billion.
These figures may be outdated, but the positive estimate of the contents of the field are 680 million barrels. The minister indicates that has since gone up with a probability of 890 million barrels. The minister can bring these figures up to date as there may have been improvement.
There has been some degree of cynicism in Newfoundland and Labrador as to whether this project was ever going to go. This is not unexpected when one remembers that the Hibernia was first discovered in 1979. Nevertheless, since 1984 when the present administration headed by the Prime Minister took over, there has been steady progress. It is not a question of there being just promises, there has been considerable performance.
I would just like to mention in that connection the fact that in 1985 Canada and Newfoundland agreed that there should be a Canada-Newfoundland offshore development fund to help Newfoundland and Labrador get ready for the development of Hibernia. That was a $300 million fund, 75 per cent being put up by the Government of Canada and 25 per cent by the Government of Newfoundland.
As of the end of last January that fund had been used for a great many projects. It was used to prepare the province and the people for the project to go ahead so that they could take the maximum advantage of it when it started. To date, the projects approved in principle amount to $132,601,000, with total costs of projects approved and approved in principle to date of $236,625,000. A great deal of that money has already been spent.
Hibernia is not merely a promise repeated by politicians. Hibernia is already performance. From that fund we have constructed the Centre for Earth Resources Research at Memorial University in Newfoundland, $27,100,000; an offshore survival centre, $5,000,000; skills training projects, $3,000,000; computer aided design facility in engineering, $1,150,000; the centre for Cold Ocean Resources Engineering, $5,000,000; the Centre for Excellence in Marine Signal Processing, $7,400,000.
These are not projects for creating temporary jobs. These are all devoted to the long-term training of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, the young people who will be trained in these kinds of facilities.
Other projects include the Offshore Technology Transfer Opportunities Program, $3,000,000; Petroleum Technology Training Programs, $21,100,000; access road to the Cow Head Oil Rig Repair Facility in Placentia Bay, $614,000; the Institute for Marine Dynamics and the new wave generator, owned by the Government of Canada in St. John's, $3,500,000; the Marine Offshore Simulator Training Centre, $12,818,000. On and on it goes, moneys expended from this fund, provided principally by the Government of Canada with a substantial contribution by the Government of Newfoundland.
Approved in principle is $34,500,000 to enhance the offshore fabrication capability of Maiystown shipyard, the great Newfoundland shipyard in Placentia Bay. The sum of $95 million is being committed to the construction of the gravity-based structure and the main support frame facility for Hibernia. This is $95 million to ensure that the gravity-based structure, along with other facilities, the main support frame facilities, the top-side facilities and the like can be constructed in Newfoundland. As a matter of fact the main site is going to be at Bull Arm in Trinity Bay in the district of the hon. member sitting opposite, Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. It is just a mile or two from the great district of St.
June 7, 1990

John's West and Placentia Bay, not far from the Bull Arm area.
This is going to be a great shot in the hon. gentleman's Bull Arm. It will be a great employment generator in the area of Placentia Bay and the district of St. John's West, in fact in all of eastern Newfoundland, and I hope in all of Newfoundland, Quebec, Ontario, and Alberta, which will be the other main centre.
We are dealing with a project that is imperial in size and concept, difficult to carry out and execute. But I think that Mobil and its associated companies have the people who can pull off this construction feat and get this field going. But they cannot do it, because of the frontier conditions under which he project must go ahead, without the assistance of the people of Canada, through the Government of Canada, with the $2.7 billion and other means as described in the bill that is now before the House.
There was a change of government in Newfoundland a year ago last April and former Premier Peckford was associated with the great battle to ensure that Newfoundland had at least joint management of this offshore resource. Mr. Peckford did not run in the last election and was succeeded by Premier Wells who led the Liberal Party to victory in April, 1989. Mr. Wells is in the capital today in connection with the Meech Lake Constitutional Conference.
Premier Wells said, and I really do not think he can be serious, but he did say publicly several times that this project was the equivalent of two fish plants being established in Newfoundland. That misses the point entirely.
I do not have the exact employment creation figures but I believe that during construction there will be approximately 35,000 jobs connected with the project. Once it is finished and the field is producing, direct employment will be in the area of 1,100.
That, of course, is directly on the project, but there will be dozens upon dozens and hundreds and thousands of Newfoundlanders employed in companies servicing the development and servicing further developments
Government Orders
that will come once Hibernia is established. A lot of those jobs will be high tech, very skilled jobs, just as they have been from the beginning.
We have dozens and dozens of entrepreneurs in Newfoundland who have prepared themselves, many of them with the help of government, for the opportunities that will come with this development.
This is a development not just in the economic interests of Newfoundland and Labrador, or the other parts of the country I have mentioned. It is a project in the national interest because it is in the national interest to overcome regional disparity in Newfoundland. If this project did nothing else, if it only assisted Newfoundland in overcoming regional economic disparity, it would be justified on that basis alone. But it is justified as well in developing a frontier offshore oil resource that Canada is going to need in the future as our on-land and more easily accessible oil and gas resources are steadily used up.
It is in the national interest that this development should go forward. It is certainly in the interest of overcoming regional disparity and of advancing regional economic equality in Canada that this project go forward.
Where are we at the moment? We are completing negotiations with the Government of Newfoundland and with the Mobil consortium as to what proportion of this great project must be carried out, from the benefits point of view, in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador; what must be carried out in the nation of Canada; just what these benefits are; and, how the benefits are going to be distributed in that manner. I think we are at the end of that process. Good progress has been made. We have to go on to see. There has to be a test on the market to see whether a lender risk-sharing arrangement is viable when it comes to financing and issuing the bonds that will be required to finance the project, from time to time, as it is under way over the next few years. I believe 1996 is the year in which it is expected that production of oil from the field would start.
Those negotiations are now approaching their end. There seems to be no reason why we cannot conclude all this during the coming summer, in the next month or two. All the final documents could be signed in time for

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
this year not to be slipped when it comes to the project being accomplished.
However, for that to be the case, the Parliament of Canada has to enact this bill before we adjourn for the summer. I am hoping, and I have no reason to doubt, that we will have co-operation from the other parties in the House so that this can be accomplished. If Parliament does not enact this legislation before we rise, during the month of June, then of course we will not be back until September and there would be real doubt as to whether or not a year would be lost with reference to the Hibernia project and the project, itself, could be in some jeopardy as a result.
Therefore, I would like to ask fellow members of the House to deal with this bill as expeditiously as they think possible, keeping in mind that there is this urgency. If we hope to complete all of the documents this summer and not to lose this year, it is important for the House to deal with this bill which was introduced last November. It is not something that we are just introducing at a late date. It has been debated at second reading on December 18 and on February 9.
I do not want to take up any more of the time of the House, except to say that I am honoured that I am still in the House of Commons when this legislation goes through the House. I have supported this project since 1979. I did all I could to assist Mr. Peckford in his struggle to acquire some rights over the offshore oil and gas resources. It was a monumental struggle that he was engaged in with the government that preceded us. I intend to do what I can to work with Premier Wells to ensure that the project goes forward now because the province and the federal government have to work together for that purpose.
In closing, I want to thank the hon. minister for the fine work he has done in this connection. I hope that members of the House will co-operate with us in seeing that we do all that is necessary before we adjourn for the summer.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. minister's presentation and noted particularly his appeal for rapid consideration of the legislation.
I find it rather odd, when we have had a gestation period now of nearly nine months since this bill was first
introduced. Nine months have transpired and nothing has happened. Nine months later, at the eleventh hour, the minister stands up and says that he hopes that, now that we have sat on this for nine months, the House of Commons can set everything else aside and expeditiously deal with this one piece of legislation. I just say we will do our best. Of course, we always do. We will work as hard as we can.
I just find it odd, I must say to the minister with all due respect, and I mean that with all sincerity, that after having a piece of legislation sitting on his desk for nine months, suddenly he wants to move it in a matter of hours.
As the minister has said, it was introduced in December. Why was it not introduced again? It is the government that decides what we do in here, not the opposition. It is not the Official Opposition and not the New Democratic Party. It is the government that decides the business of the day. It has not called this business of the day for month after month after month-for nine months.
I ask my hon. friend, the minister, with all due respect, that, if this is so urgent, if this was such a high priority for the government and if this was such an important matter, why is it introduced on the day that Premier Wells is encouraged to make a decision at the First Ministers' Conference? I realize there is no association, of course. Why has the minister taken nine months to begin serious debate on this important legislation?

Madam Speaker, the hon. gentleman is suggesting, of course, that the House has not been doing anything since December or February. As far as I know, the House has had important legislation before it the whole time.
He asks why this has not been brought forward. The last time it was brought forward, the House was in the mood to pass it with the exception of a few members who did not want to see it passed on that particular occasion. I have forgotten the date.
It was the member from Juan de Fuca.

It was the member for Juan de Fuca. One could easily be accused of profanity when one mentions his district. He did not want it to go through at that particular time.
June 7, 1990

I do not want to be bellicose today. I cannot avoid being "belly-cose", but I do not want to be bellicose today. I want to be in the mood of sweet reasonableness and simply say that this is not connected, of course, with anything that is going on in Ottawa today.
If the hon. member knew Premier Wells, he would know that it would be a wrong tactic to try either to encourage or discourage him. He told me that the Constitution was for 1,000 years. Hibernia is not for 1,000, it is only going to be for 20 or 25. He has a long-term view of the Constitution. Frankly, I think that Meech Lake will be forgotten long before Hibernia is. However, that remains to be seen.
The legislation that the province is required to pass is being debated in the Newfoundland House of Assembly now. I think the timing is right in both Houses. My hon. friend from British Columbia happens to be lucky enough to live in one of the booming parts of the country. Of course, they have had good government there for a number of years-

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I want to correct the hon. minister. I think he has his politics wrong. The Social Credit Party has been in office in British Columbia for the past few years.

Madam Speaker, on this same matter, I took the minister to imply that the government's hands would be tied in proceeding with further negotiation as required, or even with the disbursement of certain funds relating to the project, if this bill did not make it out of the Commons today or before the summer adjournment.
I am a little puzzled. If this is, indeed, his contention, would he be so kind as to inform the Minister of Finance of these requirements so that the Minister of Finance may stop securing rented accommodation, hiring staff, and renting and purchasing machinery and equipment for the purpose of implementing the GST, which, as we all know, has not yet cleared this Parliament?

Madam Speaker, with respect to the Hibernia project, this legislation authorizes the government to do certain things which it cannot do unless the House of Commons approves the legislation. Unless I am advised mistakenly, the government cannot sign the
Government Orders
final agreements or execute final agreements without the legislation being passed first.
With respect to the offshore development fund, the spending from it has been approved from year to year in the Estimates and the budget.
With respect to signing and executing agreements, giving guarantees, and doing what the government agreed to do in July, 1988, we need the approval of the House. That is why it is important. If the legislation is not passed before we adjourn, then we will not be able to do anything until next fall and a year will slip from the construction schedule.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso-Scotia Synfuels Project; the hon. member for Chambly-Riding of Laurier-Sainte-Ma-rie; and the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake-Canada Post.
Resuming debate. The hon. member for Bonavista- Trinity-Conception.

Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by congratulating my colleague from Newfoundland, the hon. Minister of International Trade, on the history and background of this project that is so important to Canada, to Atlantic Canada, and, in particular, to Newfoundland.
This project is about jobs, technology, and energy. As far as Newfoundland is concerned, it is about hope. Where hope is involved, I am not interested in being bellicose or in laying blame. I am not interested in political rhetoric. I am interested in getting this bill through the House of Commons so we can get on with this hope and make the hope a realistic thing, as opposed to the hope that it has been for almost 20 years now.
In as brief a time as possible, I would just like to recapture some of the background to demonstrate the tortuous history that this project has had. One may consider it a relatively short time, but if one is looking at it as an item of hope, it has been fairly tortuous.
The field itself is located 315 kilometres southeast of St. John's. The oilfield covers about 20,000 acres and the last capacity I saw was in the range of 600 to 900 million barrels. When capacity production starts, this amounts to

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
roughly 100 million barrels, but the daily production would be somewhere in the vicinity of 120 million barrels a day.
That is impossible.
One hundred and twenty million barrels a day?
One hundred and twenty thousand barrels a day.

One hundred and twenty thousand barrels a day. One of the things we are really concerned about is the total capacity.
As far as the hope is concerned, I would like to translate this into jobs and what it means to Atlantic Canada, indeed to the whole of Canada.
In fact, the exploration activities took place as far back as 1971, but there were really no successes until Hibernia was discovered. The exploratory drilling began in May of 1979, and it was by Chevron Standard in partnership with Mobil, Gulf, then Petro-Canada and Columbia.
In August of the same year, oil was discovered and a series of evaluation wells were drilled between then and 1984. From 1985 to July of 1988, a series of project-owner cost estimates, government proposals and tax reforms were exchanged between the parties. Then on the magic of July 18, 1988, a series of project-owner cost estimates and a series of statements of principles were discussed and signed in St. John's, Newfoundland by Prime Minister Mulroney and the then Premier of Newfoundland, Premier Peckford, together with the Government of Canada, the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador, Chevron Canada Resources, Columbia Gas Development, Gulf Canada, Mobil Oil and Petro-Canada. These were the organizations involved in the initial findings.
I recall that day. I was in St. John's and I believe the hon. minister was there as well. It was a day of jubilation across all sectors of Newfoundland. It cut across party politics, it cut across everything. It was a day of rejoicing for Newfoundland because the crisis in the fishery had arrived and as we are all aware in this House, it has got considerably worse since then. We felt that things were going to get better.
In the words of Premier Peckford at the time-and it may have been overstated-it was an indication of the way Newfoundland felt about this. He talked about the
sun shining and "have-not will be no more". That was based on something tangible happening on March 31 of the next year, 1989. March 31 came, and for reasons that I think are well known by the House, to our great disappointment, the agreement could not be signed.
We are looking at a delay of a year and a bit. During this time, we have had considerable discussion in this House. If my figures serve me right, the first reading took place on November 7. Some discussion went on over those days. The second reading took place on February 9. That is roughly four months ago. And we had some discussion just before we closed at Christmas time.
The purpose of the bill is to give the federal government the statutory authority to enter into a legally binding agreement based on the statement of principles put together in July of 1988 and subsequently negotiated between the Government of Canada, the Government of Newfoundland and the Hibernia project owners. Essentially, the bill will allow the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, with the approval of the Governor-in-Council, to enter into one or more agreements on behalf of the federal Crown in respect of the development project itself.
I think it is safe to say that the reserves of oil are not truly known. The main concern of all of us in the House is employment benefits. The construction phase will take about five or six years. It is estimated that the field will last around 20 years. During the construction phase of the projects, the partners targeted 14,500 person-years of direct Canadian employment and 32,600 person-years of indirect Canadian employment. I stress if my constituents are watching this, it talks about 14,500 for direct Canadian employment. That does not necessarily mean it will all be in Newfoundland, although we certainly hope that the majority of it will be.
Specifically, after the construction phase, the targeted Canadian employment figures-if the ones that I have are not right I know the Minister of Energy Mines and Resources will correct me-we are looking at are 1,100 direct person-years, that is those directly employed with the production and 2,450 indirect person-years. That is wild compared to the opportunities for employment that one has right now in Newfoundland and in Atlantic Canada.
June 7, 1990

With respect to the construction stage, as I understand it, the winning bidder would be able to construct a community near Come-By-Chance, as the hon. minister said, in Bull Arm. Specifically, I think it is called Mosquito Cove. They would construct a community in this area for about 2,000 employees, would pour the 500,000 tonne base, join it with the topsides and then would tow the 1.5 billion tonne gravity based structure out to its spot out in the area where it would begin production, which is roughly 315 kilometres off Newfoundland.
I recall we had an enthusiastic and a very hopeful discussion here on February 9.1 spoke to the main bill on second reading and my feeling was that we were within days of having this thing go through. In fact we were making some arrangements with the House leaders for the next week. All of a sudden we hit a little bit of a snag and there were some concerns. Whether the concerns are legitimate or not, I would like to speak to that later on. However, I was disappointed and, quite frankly, I have had a bit of a rough ride from my constituents when I go back home because they wondered what was the House of Commons doing to prevent this from going forward.
We have had enough obstacles in the way. Again I promise, and I am going to stick to that promise, that this is not a time for political rhetoric. This is a time to get on with doing something for a region of our country which is badly in need and needs this particular project. I think we should look at the positive side, while still being concerned about those aspects that have been raised by a number of my friends on the left.
Newfoundland takes its resources from the sea and whether it is fish, or whether it is oil, or whether it is the tourist attraction of the beautiful bays and villages around the area. That is what we have in Newfoundland and Labrador, and in other parts of Atlantic Canada. It is not surprising that there should be concern about the environment, and it is really this concern that is the source of the amendments that have been put forward today.
One of my party's policies is to use energy in the most environmentally responsible way. Indeed, it is my understanding that after we get through with this business and
Government Orders
we get approval, that the revised project, scaled down from the 17 to the four or five modules that have been the result of a scrubbing down to reduce the cost of this project, is going to be submitted to the Canadian Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board for approval, along with the plans for the eventual abandonment of the Gravity Bay structure. When the production is completed, we will have to win environmental approval again before Ottawa makes a decision on this. My understanding is that this environmental decision will be made by an intergovernmental body involving the Department of the Environment, the Canadian Coast Guard and Canada Oil and Gas Lands Administration.
I would suggest that when Hibernia gets that far down the pike we will have a number of options at which we can look. We could dismantle the topside and leave the structure manned. Perhaps by that time we will have found some other use for it. It would provide a structure for search and rescue, which is badly needed in that area of Newfoundland. We could take the structure down approximately 180 feet so that the largest vessel could navigate safely, or we could take the structure completely out of the ocean floor and either dismantle it or find some other use for it.
If this bill passes second reading and goes to committee, it is important that the committee concern itself with these particular concerns that have been raised by the NDP. Hopefully, we will not only be able to get this approved, but I am hoping that we can get it through committee and back for third reading before the House adjourns for the summer. Quite frankly, I do not think we can afford to wait another three months.
We have been working on this very assiduously and we have had some difficulty in getting the thing under way. Now we have reached the point where we can get something done. I would find it very difficult to support any impediments to this bill.
In the short time that I have been in this House there are many issues that have divided us. Heaven knows, we have seen so many of them here in the House. There is a place for partisanship, a time for political rhetoric, a time for being, perhaps, politically different from each other. However, I think this is one of the few issues that I have seen since I have been here where not only are members

Government Orders
anxious to approve this project but to go on record as having had their names behind approving this project. Everyone wants to get on with fuelling the hope of those people who are counting the days, in fact counting the moments, when some announcement of substance can be made and we can get on with tapping the vast reserves, and translate this into jobs, into the economy and into a working production.
Then we, in Canada, will not only be able to secure a sounder energy foundation and not have to worry about importing foreign oil, while at the same time being environmentally conscious. This will ensure the economic diversification that we have been groping for in Newfoundland since 1947. This is one of the hopes that we have. I am going to call on all members to put aside partisanship and, perhaps, the minor concerns that they might have so that this bill is approved and passes third reading before the House closes for the summer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to make a comment or two, if I might, to the Minister for International Trade and to the hon. member for Bonavista- Trinity-Conception. Let me thank both of them for the comments which they have made today.
It is not my purpose to take the time of the House, but I think possibly it is important that I just put some figures on the record so that people in the oil industry and, more importantly, the people of Newfoundland and Labrador have the latest play. If that is acceptable, I will use this opportunity to do so.
First of all, in terms of the number of barrels in the Hibernia field, members have been putting certain figures on the record and none of them are wrong because all of them have been in the public domain at one time or another. The best seismology work and information that we can put to that question is that existing reserves of Hibernia are in the range of 525 to 650 million barrels. I appreciate that while the science is specific, until one gets into the work, the actual results are subject to a fair bit of verification and one can only do that when the work is being done. The low estimate is in the order of 725 million barrels and the high estimate is one billion barrels-plus. Possibly that answers it just in quick form.
Additionally, what should be recognized is that this is light and medium crude. As our light crude, especially in the western sedimentary basin, starts declining, as it has already, there is also an additional advantage in terms of mix of crude for Canada.
The last point that I want to make is that in terms of the project now contemplated, we are looking to produce an average of 110,000 barrels of oil per day with a maximum production capacity of 150,000 barrels per day.
Madam Speaker, I was wondering if perhaps the Chair, the minister, and indeed, the House, might agree to allow questions of the minister, being that the minister has just participated in the debate.
