Madam Speaker, in rising to participate in the debate today, I would like to note that what we are debating is the reasoned amendment proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, which would have the effect of rejecting this bill for the three reasons stated. First, granting a project more than $1 billion without securing an equivalent equity in the project for the people of Canada is wrong in principle. Second, the bill fails to contain specific provisions which provide environmental protection measures in connection with the project. Third, the bill fails to contain specific provisions which provide for the creation of job opportunities in relation to the project.
These are very large topics that the reasoned amendment addresses and, in consequence, we will be dealing with each in turn through three speakers this afternoon.
June 7, 1990

I would like at the outset to make it very clear that the New Democratic Party caucus in this House opposes Bill C-44 for those reasons. We do not oppose the Hibernia project per se.
If I may draw the analogy, Madam Speaker, it may be a very good thing to have a hospital constructed in your community. Presumably everyone in your community, if there is not one there now, would be very much in favour of having a hospital constructed there.
However, if the government that proposes to build the hospital proposes to do so with straw and plasticine, your constituents are not going to be terribly thrilled at the prospect. Although the project itself may be praiseworthy and commendable and certainly worthy of public support, the form and nature that that public support takes, as well as the consequences of the form and nature of that public support, are very much a matter of attention for this House.
If the form of that support is inappropriate or inadequate, then it is the business of this House to defeat it until such time as more proper form and content are brought forward.
For these very good reasons we oppose this bill. We do not oppose job creation. On the contrary, we want jobs in Atlantic Canada. That is why we oppose the government's cuts in transfer payments. That is why we oppose the reduction in important government services in the Atlantic. That is why we oppose the government's cuts to UI. And that is why we oppose the continued mismanagement of the Atlantic fishery.
We New Democrats believe that it is vitally important to create as many jobs as possible with the money available. However, before I consider the subject of job creation in greater detail, I would like to touch on the historic background of this project and very briefly on the specific contents of this bill. Given time limitations, I will have to leave the other important subjects of economic development and environmental considerations to two of my colleagues who will be speaking a little later this afternoon.
The history of the Hibernia project has been a dizzying roller-coaster of rays of expectations and dashed hopes. When the first major oil discovery was made on the Grand Banks in 1979, the expectation was that Newfoundland would blossom to become the Norway of
Government Orders
North America. Unfortunately, the first estimates of the amount of oil in the field were soon proved to have been much too high.
In 1979, it was estimated that Hibernia contained about 1.8 billion barrels of oil. In 1985, this estimate was halved. The field was estimated to contain, as the hon. minister noted, between 800 million and 900 million barrels in all likelihood.
The estimate on the most recent Hibernia background papers is down to just 525 million to 650 million barrels. The estimates and the benefits from the project that would be enjoyed by Newfoundlanders have similarly declined steadily. Initially, many Newfoundlanders believed that the province owned this offshore resource and that it could be used mainly to provide much needed jobs and to boost the Newfoundland economy.
This hope of exclusive provincial ownership and control was dashed by the rulings of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and the Supreme Court of Canada in 1983 and 1984 respectively, rulings to the effect that the federal government has jurisdiction over this offshore mineral resource. The Atlantic Accord, a long-term agreement on the joint management of offshore oil and gas development was, therefore, signed in 1985. As Newfoundlanders know only too well, the agreement does not change the fact that Hibernia will not by itself transform the Newfoundland economy.
On top of the disappointing realization that Hibernia would not be the bonanza that many initially thought, Newfoundlanders have been disappointed that politicians have repeatedly used the promise of the project for political purposes. Politicians have regularly raised the hopes of Newfoundlanders by big, glitzy announcements of deals before or during election campaigns. The project was announced once in 1979, again in 1982 and yet again during the 1988 election when the federal Conservatives made Hibernia an important plank in their campaign in Atlantic Canada. Each time the impression was given that a final deal was done and that this would mean great things for Newfoundland.
Listen to what the Prime Minister said during a pre-election speech in St. John's on July 18, 1988. I quote: "Hibernia has been the dream of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador for decades". Given that

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
he said this nine years after it was discovered, that is a bit hyperbolic, but let it pass.
"Today the dream has been realized". During the last election campaign on October 6, 1988 the Prime Minister waxed lyrical about the project, saying, and again I quote: "For me, Brian Mulroney, Hibernia meant a lot more than barrels of oil. Hibernia to me was about dignity. Hibernia is about the future, about jobs for our kids. It is about a new tomorrow".
For his part the hon. minister of trade who spoke earlier this afternoon told more than 1,000 invited guests in St. John's on July 18, 1988 that the announcement "has nothing to do with politics. This has to do with justice". That was in 1988. That was yet another announcement that has come to very little after it was made. It is no surprise that Newfoundlanders are just a wee bit cynical about Hibernia announcements and just a mite suspicious about what repeatedly appears to them to be political opportunism of the first order.
Speaking of healthy cynicism, Newfoundlanders will recall the minister of trade has already suggested that the Opposition is somehow to blame for holding up this bill. This is a minister of a government that did not hesitate to use its majority in the House of Commons to stifle debate and ram through the hated GST, and that out-voted the Opposition to cut VIA Rail, to chop transfer payments and to slash UI benefits. This is the same government that introduced this bill on Hibernia last November 7 and then delayed further consideration of it until December 18, then until February 9 and finally, until today, a full seven months since the bill was introduced.
The government will still try to blame Hibernia delays on everyone but itself claiming that we are against jobs for Newfoundlanders, that we are against the Hibernia project itself. This is not true. We, New Democrats, do not oppose Hibernia. Again I say, we oppose this bill.
What is in Bill C-44? In a nutshell, Bill C-44 is meant to give the federal government the statutory authority to enter into one or more legally binding agreements based on the statement of principle signed in July 1988 and on the results of subsequent negotiations. It essentially sets out how the federal government will spend money on this project.
We are talking about a great deal of money. The bill proposes that the federal government contribute up to $1.04 billion toward capital costs in free grant money; up to $1.66 billion in loan guarantees for the capital project; $175 million in loan guarantees for a temporary financing facility; $300 million as a loan and no cap on the amount contributed as interest on the $1.66 billion in loan guarantees should interest become payable in consequence of those guarantees. In sum, this bill proposes that the federal government pay up to $1.04 billion in absolutely free grant money and up to $300 million as a loan and at least $1,835 billion in loans and interest guarantees for a total potential outlay of up to $3,139 billion or more. That is a lot of money.
The question we have to ask ourselves in considering this bill is: Is it a wise use of money? Does it provide the most jobs and economic development that can be had for the money?
In the rest of the short time available to me to speak today, I would like to focus if I may on the employment opportunities that will result from Hibernia if this bill passes without change.
The people of Newfoundland and Labrador need jobs.
Nobody in this House disputes that it is indeed incumbent on the Canadian confederation to come to the aid of the people in Newfoundland and Labrador to the degree necessary to bring them up to some kind of economic equality with the rest of the country. It is the contention of other people who have spoken here this afternoon that not only will Hibernia do that, but Hibernia is virtually the only vehicle that can do that.
It is true that the people of Newfoundland and Labrador need jobs. They need real economic development. Hibernia could help provide that but it is not likely to happen with this bill. Indeed, the terms of this bill will necessarily see a great many potential benefits to Newfoundland and Labrador squandered. In fact, this bill provides inadequate employment opportunities for Newfoundlanders for the public money invested and given away. Even Premier Clyde Wells recognized this publicly, pointing out in an interview published on October 2, 1989, in The Financial Post, that the number of permanent jobs generated by Hibernia would be about the size of the workforce of two fish plants.
June 7, 1990

The hon. Minister for International Trade disputed that contention earlier this afternoon. If he looks at the job creation figures involved, the 35,000 person-years created over the entire projected 25-year life of the project with construction and operation, if you take those person-years and you divide that by the 25 years, you will wind up with a figure of about 2,000 jobs a year. That is about the size of two decent fish plants. As Mr. Wells put it at that time on October 2, 1989, in The Financial Post: "The former government painted it as a saviour", he said. "It isn't."
The current estimates of job creation are much lower than the consortium that Premier Peckford predicted in the early 1980s. The 1989 Hibernia background papers suggested that up to 10,000 person-years of direct employment could be created in Newfoundland during the construction phase, and another 25,000 person-years of indirect employment and that makes up those 35,000 person-years during the construction phase. It is estimated that the 20-year operational phase will see the creation of 1,100 permanent jobs.
As the Federation of Labour President, Bill Parsons, pointed out in an interview published in the July 19, 1988 edition of The St. John's Evening Telegram'. "Those jobs are just a fraction of what is needed to turn the province's struggling economy around. As he put it, and again I quote: "The thing is there are 40,000 Newfoundlanders out of work and we won't get any revenue from Hibernia for 15 years".
In addition, some observers who suggested that because jobs are urgently needed in Newfoundland, the government's emphasis should shift to creating jobs more quickly by tapping the existing Terra Nova discovery, reportedly a much less complicated venture, leaving the more difficult Hibernia field for later.
This leaves but one alternative available. Hibernia jobs will be enormously expensive. Even if we use the government's own figures, which we know to be optimistic, Hibernia is a very expensive way of creating jobs. For example, let us use the figures published in the Hibernia background papers. These figures we know to be overestimates because they do not take into account the recent design changes. Redesigning the project to reduce costs by assembling the Topsides rig in five 'supermodules' rather than the 18 to 20 smaller components
Government Orders
originally planned could mean the loss of 10,000 construction jobs in and around St. John's. Let us be very generous and use these earlier more optimistic figures anyway.
On page 9, this 1989 government document states that for both the temporary construction period and the production period and I quote: "The combined total direct employment for residents of Newfoundland will be in the order of 32,000 person-years over the entire life of the project".
The total government involvement is $3,139 billion. That makes almost $100,000 of government money alone for the creation of every person-year of work. If we assume a 37.5 hour work week and a 50-week work year, that works out to over $50 an hour for the work. Let us be clear, that is not what people will be paid, that is the amount of public money the government is proposing to invest or spend to create that job. That is $50 an hour in government money alone, Madam Speaker.
As Newfoundland and Labrador New Democrat leader Cle Newhook put it, and I am quoting from an article in the September 15, 1980 edition of The Evening Telegram, he said:
It looks like an incredibly expensive way of creating a few jobs up
front and a few industrial jobs during production while making the
companies rich.
This is a telling and accurate assessment in my opinion. There are not many Newfoundlanders who would not agree that there are literally thousands of community economic development projects featuring hundreds of thousands of well paying jobs that can be created for the same outlay of money. In fact, when it comes to maximizing the number of jobs or getting the biggest bang for the buck, Hibernia does not stack up very well against other existing programs in the region.
Between 1984 and 1988 just over $14.5 million was spent by the provincial and federal governments under the CEIC, fisheries and rural development programs and the like, creating 775 person-years of work. That works out to just under $19,000 in government spending for every job. That is less than one-fifth of the cost per job that can be expected under the most optimistic predictions for Hibernia.
Allow me to quote at length an article from The Financial Times of July 25, 1988. The article was written

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
by William Mackness, the Dean of the Faculty of Management at the University of Manitoba. He writes:
As a regional development scheme, the project may have some merit, but not in terms of capital cost per job. Energy is one of the world's most capital-intensive industries and, accordingly, is a strikingly expensive vehicle with which to deliver regional employment. Temporary construction jobs in Newfoundland will carry a capital cost in excess of $500,000 per job. Permanent production jobs will carry a capital cost of several million dollars per job. Granted, the oil is there, but it would be difficult to find a more expensive way to deliver either oil or jobs in Newfoundland.
But, expensive or not, 32,000 person-years of work sounds like a lot of jobs.
Unfortunately Hibernia is primarily an energy project. It is not designed to be a job creation project. It will not provide nearly the boost the province needs, especially when one considers the funding and service cuts the Mulroney Conservatives have made since coming into office.
The Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council issued a report on Hibernia in July 1988. The 30-page report states that Hibernia "covers only one of the many aspects of economic growth possibilities in Newfoundland".
I would like to emphasize that point: "only one of the many aspects of economic growth possibilities in Newfoundland". When the hon. minister stands up as he did earlier this afternoon and says it is Hibernia or nothing, it is he who is betokening a terrible and even tragic lack of faith in the initiative and indeed the entrepreneurial zeal of Newfoundlanders.
In fact that same report, the CEIC advisory council report of July 1988, goes on to say that at least 70,000 permanent jobs are needed to bring Newfoundland's employment and economic figures up to the national average, just to the national average. That report was issued before the latest devastation in the Atlantic fishery.
Hibernia jobs will also be dangerous jobs. No one needs to be reminded of that awful night eight years ago, February 15, 1982, when 84 people, including 54 Newfoundlanders, lost their life when the world's largest semi-submersible drilling rig, the Ocean Ranger, capsized and sank in 18-metre lashing waves in a screaming 145-kilometre per hour wind.
There have been changes to procedures and safety equipment since then. Some people suggest that such a tragedy could never happen again. Other people are deeply concerned that we have let our guard down on safety since the Ocean Ranger disaster. The fact remains that offshore drilling takes place in one of the most inhospitable and dangerous places in the world. Offshore drilling jobs, by their very nature, are dangerous. Clearly we need to make worker safety a priority. This should include a review of the precise details of the provisions for worker safety on the Hibernia project before it proceeds.
Offshore jobs are also very stressful. According to a recent government and industry financed study, offshore oil jobs mean month-long shifts at sea, $60 for a five-minute phone call home, and a work environment some compare to a prison or a war zone.
This 118-page report based on a survey conducted in 1985 and entitled Family Life Adaptations to Offshore Oil and Gas Employment concluded that 40 per cent of women married to rig workers and nearly 20 per cent of married men working on offshore rigs were deeply unhappy with their jobs. What is even worse, many of these jobs could also go to Americans because of the free trade deal. The Mulroney Conservatives signed a deal that specifies that U.S. firms have, and I quote from the deal, "a right of national treatment". Remember that, John, the right of national treatment in seeking business opportunities.
That means that the Hibernia companies cannot discriminate against U.S. firms under the trade deal, and that means governments cannot insist on local employment and procurement guarantees. As a result, the target of 45 per cent to 50 per cent Newfoundland content in jobs and procurement-and do not forget that is the target 45 per cent to 50 per cent, half of jobs and procurement benefits-will remain just that, a target. This cannot be guaranteed because it runs directly contrary to the provisions of the free trade agreement.
In any event, the Canadian content rules in the Hibernia agreement were relaxed in the summer of 1988. Instead of regulations the Hibernia deal translated Canadian content goals of previous Hibernia policies and the Atlantic Accord into targets-again, targets not regulations-which are stated so generally that they
June 7, 1990

permit wide open bidding, but this too is required by the free trade agreement.
I am trying to keep within my time here. Before I run out of time, I want to focus on one way in which the Hibernia project demonstrates this government's ongoing, indeed continuous, stunning hypocrisy. We will remember that the Mulroney Conservatives campaigned in 1984 on a promise to provide jobs, jobs, jobs. They now claim to support this bill in part because it will create jobs, albeit expensive ones, in a region that desperately needs employment. At the same time, the Conservatives have proceeded to destroy existing job opportunities by cutting federal transfer payments, slashing VIA, closing rural post offices, closing CFB Summerside, and continually failing to address effectively the long-standing crises in the fishing industry. Then, to top it off, they slash unemployment insurance benefits for those people who do lose their jobs.
The people of Newfoundland and Labrador do not want yet another set of politicians dangling visions of prosperity in front of them. They do not need smoke and mirrors. They do not need more raised hopes and dashed expectations. They need well paying, long-term jobs- lots of them. It is about time their government began a concerted effort to assist them to achieve what they need, what they want, what they deserve.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just want to make a comment following the intervention by the hon. member for Edmonton East.
First of all the hon. member mentioned job creation. He has heard many times in this House since September 1984 that approximately 1.6 million jobs on a net basis have been created by the economy during the tenure of this government.
The hon. member should just give some attention to this since he comes from a province that is energy rich, a province that recognizes more than possibly any other province that government policies can seriously damage the resource and the jobs related to that resource. He and I might disagree on the philosophical basis in terms of development of energy resources, but what he and I should not disagree on is that the energy economy, by
Government Orders
and large, has been an engine of growth particularly for his province. He should remember that, regardless of the political differences we might have in this House.
He also should recognize, regardless of partisan differences, that all of us have been concerned, for example, that the resources belong to the provinces and that the provinces and the people in those provinces get the maximum benefit from the ownership of those resources. He should also remember that resources regarding the offshore only were clarified with the accords, and particularly the Atlantic Accord, to which my hon. colleague the Minister for International Trade referred in his comments.
I say to the hon. member, let us look in committee at the differences we have. Let us look at the rationale for Hibernia, but at end of day let us remember that permanent jobs are not created by government or by governments transferring tax points or tax dollars. Those are needed for basic services. That is why the federal government and the provincial governments agree with equalization and Established Programs Financing. Let us not hinder the people of Newfoundland and Labrador from having the permanent jobs which he talks about, as well as the benefit of resources which that part of the country needs.
If anything has impressed me as minister of energy, it is when I go to St. John's particularly and Newfoundland and Labrador generally. The people there are no different from any other Canadians. What they want is the development of their resources to be done properly and prudently. At the end of day they want to have permanent jobs based on the merits of the case, not simply on the largesse that might come from Ottawa or other taxpayers. They are no different from anyone else. This project, while not being the panacea for all ills in Newfoundland and Labrador, it goes some distance in meeting that objective.

Madam Speaker, I agree with some of what the hon. minister has just said. I agree that it is not for the government to attempt to put everybody in Newfoundland on the dole, definitely not. It is the proper role of the Government of Canada to foster and encourage that economic development in

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
Newfoundland which will result in stable, long-term, well paying jobs. There is no question of that.
As long as we are remembering things, let us remember not to be mesmerized by the prospect of oil megaprojects. I come from a province which has had a great deal of experience with oil megaprojects. I come from a province with a great deal of experience with energy as the engine of growth. Madam Speaker, I can tell you it can be the engine of destruction for many. I can tell you that when the price of oil collapsed in 1985 somewhere between 15,000 and 40,000 Albertans lost their jobs and had their lives wrecked in consequence.
Beware of oil megaprojects. Beware of the energy economy. If ever you have the alternative, if you are talking about the expenditure of public funds, not loans but direct expenditures, direct free grant money, I would advise you to look long and hard at other possibilities because among other things a great deal of that expenditure will be to the benefit of people who do not live anywhere in this country. We are told that a great deal of the production from Elibernia could be destined to go straight to the United States and never see a Canadian refinery.

Madam Speaker, I want to ask the member for Edmonton East whether he could be clear and tell the House, given all the concerns he has raised during the course of his remarks in this debate and looking at the amendments that are set out here, whether or not the NDP in essence is saying that this project ought to be put on hold. Is that what he is saying? I think the House should be clear on it.

Madam Speaker, especially for reasons that will be outlined in far greater detail by my colleague from Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing, the NDP is saying that this bill is sufficiently flawed to warrant its defeat regardless of what one thinks of the Hibernia project itself. The principal problem is the proposal to give away more than $1 billion in government money without taking a penny in equity in return. That is the main problem, but there are others.
The Hibernia project itself, if we assume it to be a worthy vehicle in the energy market which is apparently the yardstick used by the government and the Official Opposition these days, fine, no problem. But to give away $1 billion in an area that could profit from that
scale of government investment much more in other areas is to fatally flaw the bill in our opinion.

Madam Speaker, I will have my own remarks with respect to the member's position in a moment in my speech, but I want to ask him a question about the principle of not putting money in without taking equity in a project. I happen to think that Hibernia benefits all of Canada. It benefits the nation, assists in the area of self-efficiency, and is good for the whole country.
But putting that aside for a moment, given this principle of cancelling the project if there is $1 billion and no equity, is the member saying that, in the case of the farmers of western Canada who have received each year over the last four or five years approximately $1 billion of federal assistance, it is the position of the NDP that the government should take equity in their farms or no assistance should be forthcoming? I am interested in hearing what he has to say in the House.

Madam Speaker, the analogy is completely unreasonable. It does not apply. It is not individual Newfoundland oil producers who are heading out to the Hibernia site and digging up pails of oil and taking it in.
Nor, Madam Speaker, is it individual Newfoundland oil producers who work that field, sometimes for generations, building up an economic base that is fundamental to the survival of Canada as a whole.
No, there is no comparison between the two. Mobil Oil does not farm in western Canada.
Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International
TVade): The hon. gentleman for Edmonton East says he supports this project. I hope to God he does not support any other projects that I am interested in, if he thinks stopping the bill will make the project possible. The people of Newfoundland have waited 11 years for this project. The hon. member supports the project, but, by golly, he is going to stop this bill going through the House so that he can really show the people of Newfoundland and Labrador how he supports the project. Tcilk about logic!
What about the question of jobs and comparing this to two fish plants or whatever. This is not just a question of the jobs that may be created directly by this project, and a great many jobs are going to be created directly by the project, it is a question of changing the nature of the
June 7, 1990

economy of Newfoundland so it is not dependent just on the fishery or on some jobs in pulp and paper.
It is to give the people another alternative, highly skilled jobs, not just the jobs out there on the rigs or in construction, or the jobs at Bull Arm, although we hope there will be more fields.
There is the Terra Nova field. There is the White Rose field and there are indications of other fields out there. Hopefully they will be able to construct rigs and so on at Bull Arm for another 50 or 60 years, as well as in the Newfoundland dockyard and the Marystown shipyard where we are putting $34.5 million with the province so that they can take full advantage of this.
It is not just the direct jobs. It is all of the companies that have been created in the last 10 or 12 years, the high technology companies and the kind of jobs they are going to be able to provide. Anyone who wants to compare this with another two fish plants for Newfoundland has something wrong with their mental processes or does not have sufficient scope to visualize what this is going to do.
I do not think for a moment that Premier Wells meant it. This is not creating 500 more jobs for women to go on a fish line and cut fish. This is not the kind of job this process is going to create, or jobs for 12 or 14 weeks of the year in an inshore fish plant and those types of jobs, though God knows they are welcome enough.
I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that he and his party take a different approach to this. They are supposed to be the party that represents the labour movement and the like. When they have an opportunity to support a bill that is going to change the nature of the economy of Newfoundland and create some better paying, more skilled work, they oppose it. How else is this going to start if the government does not assist in getting it started?
If the NDP is going to vote against any assistance to the project, then how is the project ever going to start? If the NDP supports this project which took 11 years of struggle to get this far, they cannot really come down to Newfoundland and tell how helpful they were if they are going to vote against this bill and do everything they can to stop it going through the House.
Government Orders

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is now over. Resuming debate. The hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte.

Madam Speaker, I must say to the member for Edmonton East who spoke on behalf of the New Democratic Party that I am really quite amazed at the attitude of the New Democratic Party with respect to the Hibernia development. More particularly, I am quite amazed at the attitude of the new Democratic Party about Newfoundland and Newfoundlanders. I frankly find it patronizing. I find it insulting, if not by design, I hope at the very least that it must be by accident, to the intelligence of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador.
The Hibernia project is not something new that materialized as a matter of debate before this House at the first reading of Bill C-44 on November 7, 1989. This project, its potential, its development, has been around for a long time, several decades.
I want to tell the hon. member who has been here for less that two years-and I am not reflecting upon him in any way, as he has been an active and engaged member all the time he has been here. The debate we are attempting to have today has its genesis in a debate between jurisdictions several decades ago. Certainly that debate has gone on in an intense fashion for the last decade.
I have to tell him in all frankness that to have an hon. member from Edmonton East, as well-intentioned in his own mind as he might be, stand and purport to speak for the people of Newfoundland, to understand the history and dynamics of this project and suggest that he and his party are going to save Newfoundland from a tragic mistake, I find patronizing and insulting. It displays an abysmal ignorance of the history of this development and the kind of agreements that have been negotiated and understandings that have been reached over a very long and difficult debate.
What do we have at the end of a very difficult and long process, sometimes a partisan process between parties and sometimes a difficult process between jurisdictions? We have at the eleventh hour the New Democratic Party storming into the House of Commons and suggesting

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
that they are going to put the brakes on an important project not only for Newfoundland but for Canada. That is an incredibly patronizing attitude.
Let me say, in all sincerity, that this is not the kind of approach we expect from the New Democratic Party. It is not the normal thing we see in this place. I find the member's attitude absolutely incredible, because what is Bill C-44?
I find the attitude incredible. I listened in silence to the hon. member and he ought to listen in silence to me. What is Bill C-44? The Canadian public has listened to a lot of rhetoric. In reality, it is a piece of enabling legislation. That is all it is, enabling legislation. It makes possible agreements. It makes possible the participation of the federal government with two other partners, one being the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador and the other being the private consortium.
This legislation represents the approval of Parliament for the government to participate with two other partners in an offshore oil development, the Hibernia Field specifically and other fields, if and when they have been proven viable. That is what it does. What does the New Democratic Party say? It says in essence-and I find this amusing-that it wants to impose certain conditions upon the Government of Canada-more particularly the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador which is not in this House but in another jurisdiction-and upon the private consortium. It wants the federal government to impose arbitrary conditions, without consent, knowledge, dialogue, discussion and the agreement of the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, representing the people of Newfoundland and Labrador and the consortium.
The amendment moved by the New Democratic Party asks that the bill be not now read a second time because granting the project more than $1 billion without securing equivalent equity in the project for the people of Canada is wrong in principle. There is provision in this enabling legislation for the Government of Canada to take an equity position, but it is an equity position that will arise out of negotiation with the consortium and with the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, the
two other partners in the project. That ability is contained in the enabling legislation.
The hon. member is asking the Government of Canada to move in arbitrarily, like a bull in a china shop, to state upfront what its position is going to be, notwithstanding changing circumstances. God knows, world prices change and therefore circumstances change. He wants that provision included in advance of any discussion or negotiation with the players.
That is not a reasonable amendment. That is a patronizing amendment that displays an abysmal ignorance about the agreement that has been reached between all of the partners and players in this agreement.
The second paragraph of the amendment states that the bill fails to contain specific provisions which provide environmental protection measures in connection with the project. The reality is that in 1985 the environmental review on the Hibernia project was completed. It was an extensive, veiy complex and public process. It was debated and circulated. It is debated still today, with many players and broad representation.
There has been an environmental process and there is provision on any additional or new field other than Hibernia which is being considered, for additional environmental review. I have no hesitation in saying as a member of the opposition Liberal Party that it would be subject to the full weight of guidelines that have now been laid out by the Minister of Energy. That is proper.
There is nobody in Newfoundland and Labrador, which for 500 years has depended upon the fishery, the harvest of the sea, who wants to risk the cod stocks in any way, shape or form. God knows they are in bad enough shape now because of the exploitation by man, both in this country and many other countries of the world.
We are not prepared to take that environmental risk, we have to be satisfied. The heritage of our province is the bounty of the sea. We have the patronizing attitude of the New Democratic Party, a party that rushes in at the eleventh hour, to say there must be an environmental review. There has been a review and we shall remain vigilant on the environment. To assume that that vigilance is not there, that Newfoundlanders are a people so much in a rush for a bit of prosperity that they would

turn their backs on their heritage, is an insult to the people of Newfoundland. Frankly, I find it insulting, and the hon. member ought to have known better.
The third provision in the amendment states that the bill fails to contain specific provisions which provide for the creation of job opportunities in relation to the project. Again, it is an amendment which displays a total lack of knowledge about what has gone on for 10 years and what the debate has been for 10 years between the national government, the provincial government and the consortium.
What has the debate been about? Hibernia is adjacent to the province of Newfoundland, located close to the province of Newfoundland. The debate has been about whether the benefits from that project would flow to the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. That is what the long history of conflict, over a period of time, and negotiation has been all about, governments of Newfoundland and Labrador ensuring that, within the bounds of viability, there should be some long-term, permanent benefit to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador.
We are sensitive to not having a boom and bust economy. We are sensitive to not overheating the economy, as occurred in Scotland, and seeing that the people prosper. We are sensitive to having a pace and control of development, not allowing it to be done totally by the private sector. That is why we as a province in a collective sense, essentially put away our ability to have this project six or seven years ago, earlier than it would otherwise come on stream. We said no to unplanned development. We wanted a plan; to know what the effect is on the society, the social structure, the values of our community, before we proceed.
The hon. member and his party, the New Democratic Party, now want the federal government to arbitrarily write into the bill what the pace of development will be, when the federal government is now obligated to consult with the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador regarding the pace of development. The control and the assurances for the people of our province is vested in the legislature and government of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador and the hon. member wants to take that away.
The hon. member believes that we here in Ottawa, in this gilded chamber, are somehow supreme, wise and, in our wisdom, we can do better than those people down in St. John's, that fog-infested capital, in telling them what
Private Members' Business
the pace of their development should be. The hon. member is saying, "We in the New Democratic Party, given our usual bleeding-heart consideration for those unfortunate, unintelligent people, unable to help themselves, we will determine here in Ottawa, from this ivory tower, what their pace of development will be, because they cannot help themselves".

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE REGIONAL RATES OF PAY
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE REGIONAL RATES OF PAY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider abolishing the Regional Rates of Pay, now in force for certain federal government employees, in accordance with its stated policy of pay equity.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on December 7 of last year, I spoke in the House on a very regressive piece of back-to-work legislation, Bill C-49. That will go down in the history of this Parliament as one of the most regressive, callous attacks on organized labour in Canada in recent history. I said at that time that I would hope that never again in this Parliament would I have to address the House on the discriminatory wage practice called regional rates of pay.
The government opposite has not listened to logic. The government shows no change of attitude at all in its perpetuation of discriminatory wage practices that primarily affect those individuals who live on the east coast of Canada.
Here is a little bit of history about regional rates of pay for anybody out there who is watching and wants to know what it is all about. Regional rates of pay have been practised by governments for a number of years. Over that period of time governments of the day put in a

June 7, 1990
Private Members' Business
system of regional rates of pay, probably reflecting society's view that it was all right to pay people based not on the work that they did, but on where they lived. There was all kinds of rationale used at the time, but most important of all, one has to understand that it was acceptable behaviour 27 years ago to do that.
The many times when I have raised the issue of regional rates of pay in this place, I received the rebuttal from the government members that previous Liberal governments did the same thing. We are now into 1990. What society may have accepted in 1957 is not necessarily what society will accept today.
The government's rhetoric on pay equity has been incredible. Time and time again we have government members speaking in the House and different mouthpieces of the government outside of the House talking about the government's commitment to pay equity.
Pay equity means equal pay for work of equal value, but time and time again in this place, in committees, and in public, when asked if it supports abolishing regional rates of pay, the government has said no, it does not support abolishing regional rates of pay.
Only 18 or 20 months ago, during the federal election campaign, we had a potential strike situation develop in a very important part of the public service. It was the CBRT and GW, the dockyard workers. On the east coast, there were over 1,500 men and women who work in the employ of the Government of Canada in the dockyards in Halifax and Dartmouth.
At that particular time, the primary issue that almost forced a strike was the issue of regional rates of pay. Quite simply, what the union was looking for, and what the men and women who worked in the CBRT and GW down on the east coast were looking for, was not a lot of money. They were not looking for great changes to their work environment. What they were looking for was fairness and equality. What they wanted was pay equity with their brothers and sisters working for the same employer, the Government of Canada, doing the same job, with the same job description on the west coast.
But the government dug in its heels and told them no, and there were offers going back and forth across the
table. Eventually, in the middle of the election campaign, there was an offer on the table which perpetuated the regional rate of pay and perpetuated that discriminatory wage gap.
Unfortunately, the vast majority of Canadians who oppose the government-now 85 per cent-would now say unfortunately the Conservative government managed to bluff its way into another electoral term, one that will most likely be its last electoral term.
After the government got that term, it basically blackmailed the union. It told the union that the offer on the table during the election campaign would get worse, because now it had another term and it did not like what the union had been saying about the federal Tory policies in this regard. The union had better darn well accept it, and accept it now, because the offer would get worse.
Those individuals who were working at the dockyards in Halifax, in my humble opinion, are no less worthy of their pay for their day's labour than the people who are working on the west coast in the Victoria shipyards. The government insisted on perpetuating disparity based, not on colour, not on religion, or not on language of choice, but based on where people live in the country.
When we talk about pay equity and the need for the government to remove immediately regional rates of pay, we are talking about a matter of equality. That is what it boils down to.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE REGIONAL RATES OF PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is proposing that the government consider abolishing the regional rates of pay now in force for certain government employees in accordance with its stated policy of pay equity. I respect the hon. member's sincerity, but from his remarks I still sense a little confusion.
I want to concentrate on the mistaken impression that the hon. member has that regional rates of pay and pay equity are somehow one and the same. They certainly are not. In fact, I recall the hon. member was told that quite explicitly by the President of the Treasury Board during debate on Bill C-49.
I think that a review of the Canadian Human Rights Act will help make it clear to the hon. member that what he calls pay equity is distinct from regional rates of pay. This act spells out what the federal government, as an employer, must carry out in order to eliminate discrimination, and in this particular context pay discrimination. The government's policy, as has been stated many times in this House in respect to what the hon. member calls pay equity is based on section 11 of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
It may be helpful to quote section 11 of the act which
states:
It is a discriminatory practice for an employer to establish or maintain differences in wages between male and female employees employed in the same establishment who are performing work of equal value.
What do we learn from this section? We first learn that what the hon. member is referring to is not pay equity but is in fact equal pay for work of equal value. More importantly, we learn that the government as an employer shall not maintain differences in pay between male and female employees performing work of equal value. That is to say that the government shall not discriminate on the basis of pay between male and female employees performing work of equal value.
Section 11(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act does not give us any guidance as to regional rates. It merely states that there shall not be any pay discrimination based on gender. Section 11 goes on to spell out the criteria to be applied to determine the value of work including the composite of the skill, effort and responsi-
June 7, 1990

bility required in the performance of the work and the conditions under which the work is performed.
Further, section 11 deems that separate establishments established or maintained by the employer solely or principally for the purpose of establishing or maintaining differences in wages or maintaining differences in wages between male and female employees shall be considered a single establishment.
I have just paraphrased sections 2 and 2(1) of section 11 of the Canadian Human Rights Act and as yet we have seen no mention of regional rates.
I am trying to show that the hon. member has confused equal pay for work of equal value, or as he calls it pay equity, with regional rates of pay. I believe that by going through the Canadian Human Rights Act and the equal wage guidelines in a logical manner, as I have done up to now, it will be eminently clear when I have finished that the government's policy on equal pay for work of equal value is not in conflict with the government's policy on regional rates.
Let us go back to the equal wage guidelines. Sections 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15 deal with who is an employee of an establishment, complaints made under the act by individuals and complaints by groups.
The last area of the equal wage guidelines that I want to deal with is section 16 which spells out the reasonable factors that justify for the purpose of subsection 11(3) of the Canadian Human Rights Act a difference in wages between male and female employees performing work of equal value in an establishment.
I believe that this section of equal wage guidelines is terribly important and as such I intend to quote the entire subsection. However, before I do, I want to remind the House, as I have already stated, that the government's policy on equal pay for for work of equal value is based on the Canadian Human Rights Act and as such the following quote from section 16 will reinforce that the government's policy on equal pay for work of equal value is not in conflict with the government's policy on regional rates.
Private Members' Business
16. For the purposes of subsection 11(3) of the Act, a difference in wages between male and female employees performing work of equal value in an establishment justified by
(a)	different performance ratings, where employees are subject to a formal system of performance appraisal that has been brought to their attention;
(b)	seniority, where a system of remuneration that applies to employees provides that they receive periodic increases in wages based on their length of service with the employer;
(c)	a re-evaluation and downgrading of the position of an employee, where the wages of that employee are temporarily fixed, or the increases in the wages of that employee are temporarily curtailed, until the wages appropriate to the downgraded position are equivalent to or higher than the wages of that employee;
(d)	a rehabilitation assignment, where an employer pays to an employee wages that are higher than justified by the value of the work performed by that employee during recuperation of limited duration from an injury or illness;
(e)	a demotion procedure, where the employer, without decreasing the employees wages, reassigns an employee to a position at a lower level as a result of the unsatisfactory work performance of the employee caused by factors beyond the employee's control, such as the increasing complexity of the job or the impaired health or partial disability of the employee, or as a result of an internal labour force surplus that necessitates the reassignment;
(f)	a procedure of gradually reducing wages for any of the procedures set out in paragraph (e);
(g)	a temporary training position, where, for the purposes of an employee development program that is equally available to male and female employees and leads to the career advancement of the employees who take part in the program, an employee temporarily assigned to the position receives wages at a different level than an employee working in such a position on a permanent basis.
(h)	the existence of an internal labour shortage in particular job classification;
(i)	a reclassification of a position to a lower level, where the incumbent continues to receive wages on the scale established for the former higher classification; and -
Here it is, and I appreciate your waiting:
(j)	regional rates of wages, where the wage scale that applies to employees provides for different rates of wages for the same job depending on the defined geographic area of the workplace.
There it is, Mr. Speaker. Subsection (j) of section 16 of the Equal Wages Guidelines makes it perfectly clear that it is reasonable and justifiable to have a policy of regional rates while at the same time having a policy of equal pay for work of equal value.

June 7, 1990
Private Members' Business
As I stated earlier, I felt that it was quite important to quote the entirety of section 16.
I did so because I did not want to leave the impression that regional rates of pay was the only reasonable and justifiable factor that allowed a difference in wages between male and female employees performing work of equal value. Section 16 specifies 10 different reasons, including regional rates, that justify a difference in wages between male and female employees performing work of equal value. I think the answer is clear that there is absolutely no conflict between the government's policy on regional rates and the government's policy on equal pay for work of equal value. The government's policy on equal pay for work of equal value is based on the Human Rights Act where I have shown that regional rates of pay are permitted.
Let there be no mistake about the government's commitment to the concept of equal pay for work of equal value. I need only remind the House about the government's recently announced equal pay adjustments for clerical and regulatory, secretarial and education support employees. It is important to note that the employer took the incentive in making these adjustments.
While the government is committed to equal pay for work of equal value, it is also committed to its compensation policy included in which are regional rates of pay. The government's compensation policy, which has been explained many times in this House, is to compensate its employees with wages and other terms and conditions of employment that are comparable to but do not lead those employees in the private sector who do similar work. The compensation policy recognizes that the federal Public Service compensation should be sufficient to recruit and retain qualified employees. However, where there is a locally identifiable labour market and it is possible to recruit locally then the compensation policy calls for regional rates of pay. Regional rates of pay that are comparable to but do not lead those of employees in the local private sector and are sufficient enough to recruit and retain locally qualified employees.
A few examples of regional rates of pay are the general labour and trades group and the general services group. While it is true that in the context of collective bargaining with unions representing these employees, the number of pay zones have been reduced over the
years, this was done in direct reaction to local market conditions. Obviously, when it is no longer possible to identify or recruit from a local market, then market conditions demand a change in the regional pay zones to one that does reflect existing conditions.
To come back for a moment to my main theme of equal pay for work of equal value, the government's commitment to regional rates of pay does not interfere with equal pay but works in harmony with it, because it is obvious now that within any given regional pay zone equal pay for work of equal value applies and, as I have already stated and elaborated on, it does not operate between pay zones. Differences in wages for male and female employees performing work of equal value is justifiable and reasonable in terms of the Canadian Human Rights Act, but also in terms of a responsible employer, which the government certainly is.
This House has been told many times about the practice of private employers in respect of regional rates. The recognition of local labour conditions by other employers is growing yearly. I would say that the government is acting in complete concert with the private sector by paying regional rates when the local market warrants it. To do otherwise, would be a sign of an irresponsible employer.
What would be the result if the government were to abandon its policy of regional rates? What would be the affect on the local labour market? Let me note a few of the effects of such an action. Paying national rates of pay when regional rates of pay are warranted would only serve to over-pay employees in some regions and underpay employees in other regions in relation to the rates of pay prevailing in those regions.
A far more serious effect, I believe, would be the effect on the private sector in the different regions. They would be faced with the dilemma of the federal government paying national rates while their employees were paid local rates in response to local economic conditions. How could those employers possibly survive when faced with the prospect of having to raise the rates of their employees beyond what local conditions warranted in order to compete with a federal government for qualified employees.
Let me conclude by summarizing my approach to the hon. member's motion. Regional rates of pay are not in conflict with equal pay for work of equal value, but in
June 7, 1990

fact are consistent with the Canadian Human Rights Act. Regional rates of pay are part of the government's compensation policy and, as such, match the practice of private employers and respect local market conditions. They are fair, reasonable and simply make common sense.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE REGIONAL RATES OF PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the motion which was presented by the hon. member for Dartmouth concerning the payment of regional rates for certain federal government employees in view of the government's policy of pay equity.
Compensation policy for the federal Public Service since Confederation has embodied a number of guiding principles which have emerged with relative regularity and consistency. The public sector compensation must be fair to both employees and to the tax-paying public. That is very important. It must be fair to both. The Public Service compensation must be comparable to that found in the private sector, but does not materially exceed the compensation paid for similar services by private sector employers.
Public Service salaries should be sufficient to attract and retain qualified employees. In comparing the compensation paid in the federal government with the private sector for similar jobs, the terms and conditions of employment as well as the relative advantages and disadvantages of employment in the two sectors must be taken into account.
Restraint should be exercised in times of economic adversity as an example to the private and public sectors and that Public Service settlements should be fiscally responsible and contribute to the containment or the reduction of inflationary pressures.
Regional rates of pay should be established for groups where private sector data indicate significant variations and labour market rates among regions in Canada.
Compensation levels for the vast majority of the Public Service employees are established through the collective bargaining process. When collective bargaining was introduced in the Public Service in 1967, there was a concomitant revamping of the entire compensation system, including classification and pay.
In order to prepare the way for collective bargaining, the new system was designed to serve several objectives. The first was to provide a logical framework for the determination of bargaining units and a negotiation of pay rates.
The second was to make it possible for the government to respond flexibly to changes in outside rates of pay and at the same time to retain a relatively high degree of stability in the more important rate relationships between jobs and the Public Service.
The third objective was to permit different approaches to wage and salary administration and to personnel administration generally for different types of employees.
The fourth objective was to provide attractive career patterns and strong incentives to superior performance. This included the provision of classification and pay system which would support and encourage the best and most effective employment of human resources in the Public Service. Attractive career patterns marked by the absence of both artificial barriers to mobility and lateral transfers and by the opportunity for advancement by merit to higher income levels were advocated. A related objective was the provision in the pay plans of strong incentives to superior performance.

June 7, 1990

These objectives of the current compensation system, as well as the principles of government compensation policy are reflected in the legislation which currently governs employer-employee relations in the determination of compensation levels for the federal Public Service employees.
The compensation policies of different organizations vary accordingly to the objectives and goals each seeks to achieve. Within the collective bargaining context it is conventionally assumed that an organization's objective is to establish wages and benefits at a level necessary to attract and retain employees with skills and abilities sufficient to fulfil the requirements of the firm or organization. Normally this involves the payment of wages and benefits which reflect conditions prevalent in the appropriate labour market, a competitive policy.
For example, no one forces people to take a job in the Public Service. They can always look in the job market and take one with the private sector. One would assume that people take jobs in the Public Service because of the stability of employment, the pension benefits, and other benefits. What would happen if we increased the level of regional rates of pay? It would distort the local labour market and make people want to leave the private sector to go to the federal government, bidding up wages in the private sector, making them less competitive.
An analysis has been done, and I say this for my friend from Dartmouth, and it would cost the federal government $100 million. What would happen is the regional rates would rise to the highest national rate. A hundred million dollars. Now, where are we going to get that? Should we raise taxes? Is the hon. member in favour of another rate point in the GST? Where would it come from?
Does the hon. member want to distort the local labour markets all across the country, making the private sector uncompetitive? That is what the member is advocating. The member is advocating structural imbalances in our Canadian economy which bid up interest rates, inflation, and so on.
It is the structural imbalances created by the previous Liberal government through these programs which makes it harder to change the competitiveness of our
Private Members' Business
economy. We have been doing that gradually and it has been proven in the number of jobs created.
The government's aim is to pay a going rate in the labour market for the various classes of employees. The government expects a reasonably good quality of labour and it expects to pay employees fairly with respect to one another so that employees themselves feel that they are properly paid.
As I said before, and I will say this again for the hon. member's benefit, when you join the Public Service you join for a variety of reasons. One may be the stability of employment, or the pension plan, or other benefits.
Most private sector businesses do pay a regional rate of pay on a local market basis, particularly for operational, administrative and technical support jobs. The reason given most frequently by these firms for having geographic salary differentials is the nature of local salary and wage markets.
As an employer, the federal government is committed to paying rates of pay which are equitable and competitive with rates being paid outside the Public Service for similar occupations. Where the outside pay data of occupational groups indicates significant variations from the Canadian average and where the area of recruitment and the mobility of employees within the public service is limited, the government as an employer considers it appropriate to pay regional and not national rates of pay. As an employer competing with other employers, it is the government's view that the payment of regional rates contributes to the achievement of fair and competitive wages in the local market.
Currently most federal Public Service employees receive national rates of pay. However, some 30,000 employees, or approximately 16 per cent of the total Public Service workforce, are paid according to regional rates of pay.
The abandonment of regional rates of pay in the Public Service would have a negative impact on regional development and the fiscal framework. It would be very unlikely, or even undesirable, to have national rates emerge which would be based on an average of regional rates. National rates would gravitate to the highest regional rates. These rates would pose unfair competition to the private sector in the traditionally lower wage areas of Canada and would serve to dissuade industrial development in these regions. Is that what the hon.

June 7, 1990
Private Members' Business
member is asking for: less industrial development in his region? No.
Fiscally the estimated cost of moving public servants presently paid on a regional basis to a national rate is $100 million. Where are we going to get that? Are we going to raise taxes? Are we going to print money and create inflation? Is that what the hon. member wants?
As my colleague, the hon. President of the Treasury Board has stated in this House, this government is committed to maintaining regional rates of pay, where it is indicated that such an approach is in the best interests of the local labour market.
In summary, I think we want to be competitive in Canada. We do not want to distort the local labour markets. We do not want to raise taxes, which would cost us $100 million. I would say that our system is working very well now.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE REGIONAL RATES OF PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise and speak in support of the motion put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth. He proposes in his motion that "the government should consider abolishing the Regional Rates of Pay, now in force for certain federal government employees, in accordance with its stated policy of pay equity".
It has also been said that it is necessary for us to remind the government of its responsibilities as an employer and as a role model for the private sector. The government seems determined to be dragged into the 20th century, much less the 21st, kicking and screaming all the way.
As has been said here, last November we witnessed a strike by ships' crews and hospital services workers that could have been avoided if the government had respected the groups' concerns and sat down with them before the situation reached a critical stage. These people were trying to convince the government of the fundamental injustice of discriminating between workers who perform the same jobs but who live in different parts of the country or are of different genders. The government resorted to back to work legislation but still refused to acknowledge any responsibility for the terrible situation. When the conciliation board recommended that wage parity be given to these groups, the government filed a minority report objecting to the recommendations.
This attitude is shameful. If the government refuses to pay the same wages for the same job, then its so-called commitment to pay equity is a sham, as has been said before here today. We challenge the government to put its money where its mouth is. The government has made a tiny gesture toward these demands, but it is an empty gesture. Regional rates of pay differ according to zones and the general labour and trades groups have seen the number of zones reduced from 15 to 10. This is meaningless. The basic principle remains: certain people are paid less than others for doing the exact same job.
Pay equity is a thorny issue, but in this case the problem could not be clearer. The majority of trades personnel, as I said, are classified under the general labour and trades group. There are some interesting and some shocking figures to consider. The group is divided into 17 subgroups, and in 7 of the subgroups hourly wage rates in Atlantic Canada are the lowest in Canada and in 5 other subgroups they are the second lowest.
For instance, construction inspectors in the Atlantic provinces earn between $10.16 an hour and $13.30. For the same job in British Columbia, excluding metropolitan Vancouver and metropolitan Victoria, the pay is $11.82 and $15.63. What makes the job more valuable in British Columbia than it is in Prince Edward Island? This is the question Atlantic Canadians are asking. There are other examples, and they form an unmistakable pattern. An Atlantic Canadian makes less than his or her counterpart anywhere else in this huge country of ours, simply because of where he or she lives. There is no other reason.
I am sure that my colleagues on the other side of the House, and they have already done so, will rush to tell me that indeed there is very good reason for this. When the President of Treasury Board appeared before the legislative committee on Bill C-49 he said, and I quote from the minutes of the December 12 meeting: "Labour markets are not national. They are regional". This has been said here today. "If the federal government decided to pay all employees the same wages as it would
June 7, 1990

pay in downtown Toronto, it would wreck the local economies in many regions of the country".
I suggest that the government is already doing a very good job of wrecking local economies, such as that of Atlantic Canada. If this theory is sound-and since I am not an economist I will not pass judgment on that here-I say that pay equity would be but a drop in the bucket. Our regional economy is already in deep trouble largely because of federal measures such as the gutting of the UI program, the failure to renew the ERDAs, the cutbacks to ACOA, the mismanagement of the fishery, and the inadequate package offered in its place.
Some members might respond that regional rates of pay only reflect the fact that the cost of living varies between areas. I will grant you it is true that it costs less to live in some parts of Atlantic Canada than it does, for instance, in downtown Toronto, but I have other problems with this argument.
How does reducing the individual spending power do anything to help the local economy? I should think that if more money, whether in the form of consumer spending or income taxes, goes into the local economy everyone benefits.
The argument avoids the fact that workers are discriminated against because of where they choose to live and raise their family. This is just another way, as was said over here today, of preaching resettlement to Atlantic Canadians as an answer to their problems. They say: "You want to earn more money for the same job? Fine, move to Toronto and you will get it. Abandon your home. Abandon your friends. Pull up your roots". No, no, Atlantic Canadians refuse to accept this.
The minister stated, and again I quote: 'I will not in any way make a commitment that this government is going to get rid of the concept of regional rates of pay. It would not make sense".
What does not make sense and what is so offensive to workers is that the government is basically saying that some people are worth more than others. This has never been more obvious than it was last November when the east coast ships' crews were striking for wage parity with those on the west coast. Both groups risk their lives on the high seas to protect their coasts and to keep foreign fishermen from stealing even more of the fish than the government is already giving them. Both groups leave their families for months at a time to do this. According
Private Members' Business
to their pay cheques, west coast lives were more valuable than east coast lives. No matter what anybody says that is the impression left.
It is my fundamental problem with any argument against pay equity that it is a matter of dignity and of respect for the individual. Pay equity is based on responsibility, not on geography. If this government's commitment to pay equity is more than just hollow rhetoric, it will abolish regional rates of pay. The government must stop treating Atlantic Canadians as second-class citizens.
I have heard much rhetoric here today about the differences between pay equity and regional rates of pay. What it all boils down to is that people are being paid less for doing the same thing, and this is wrong. I am pleased to support this motion put forward by my hon. colleague from Dartmouth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to the motion of the hon. member for Dartmouth which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider
abolishing the Regional Rates of Pay now in force for certain regional
federal government employees, in accordance with its stated policy of
pay equity.
I feel quite qualified to speak on this matter as an employer from Atlantic Canada with a lot of experience in competing with the government for employees. I am sure the hon. member has good intentions, but in my view his motion will be very, very damaging to our economy in Atlantic Canada.
I will bet dollars to doughnuts that neither of the previous speakers have experienced the frustration and anger of losing their very best employee, the highest quality employee, the highest productive employee with years and years of training in whom they have invested or seeing them just walk away to go to a government job and leave them abandoned.
It is a frustrating experience and we cannot fight it because the private sector cannot compete with Ottawa for benefits and pay. The only way we can compete is to increase wages in our own business and sector to a level where we can compete and therefore the whole business expires and declines.
I believe it is absolutely essential to maintain equal pay for equal value in the private sector. It is interesting that the private sector with strong quality people will grow and prosper, but a government with strong quality

June 7, 1990
Private Members' Business
people will not grow and prosper and will not add wealth and jobs to the economy. It will just do the opposite.
I would challenge the members from Dartmouth and Charlottetown to take a survey of their small shop owners and small industry owners in their towns. They should ask them if they would like to compete with Ottawa for their wages and employees. Maybe they could set up a 1-800 number and have the employers call and vote as to whether they want to compete with Ottawa for their employees.
This motion does not seem to recognize that the government compensation policy for its employees already takes into account many factors, including the issue of pay equity. This government has an enormous responsibility in its role as an employer. This responsibility extends not only to its valued resource, our employees of the federal Public Service, but it extends also to the taxpayers and other important employers across the country.
It appears to me that the other speakers do not take into account the other employers. They only consider the government as an employer. For the government employees, we must pursue a policy on rates and pay that recognizes the valuable contribution made by our public servants to the delivery of government programs and the continued high quality of service delivered to the public at large.
The government's policy on compensation recognizes the following principles: First, that the terms and conditions of employment for federal public servants should be comparable to but not lead those employees in the private sector who do similar work. I ask those members to check with employers in their towns and see how they feel about that one.
Second, that comparison with the private sector shall take into consideration factors of employment such as job security, pensions, hours of work, and other benefits. Sometimes the private sector just cannot compete with these.
Third, the federal Public Service compensation should be sufficient to recruit and retain qualified employees and be determined so that appropriate compensation relationships are maintained among Public Service occupations.
Fourth, most public servants should have the right to participate in the determination of their own compensation and particular conditions of employment through responsible collective bargaining.
Fifth, federal compensation settlements will contribute to reducing inflation and be fiscally responsible.
Sixth, recognition of pay equity implementation under the Human Rights Act is based on entirely different principles from those contained in the employer's policy on compensation, that is, the Canadian Human Rights Act does not take into account either the relevant market salaries or internal organizational salary relationships. The objective of the Canadian Human Rights Act is to change purposely these relationships where there is evidence of gender or sexual discrimination.
The government's policy on rates of pay is based on a job classification system that recognizes the skills, the effort, the responsibilities, and the working conditions encountered in the employment in the federal Public Service.
It is these factors which must be scrutinized in the analysis of the appropriate level of compensation for our employees and then compared to a similar job classification in the private sector to determine if the rate of pay is comparable to that of the private sector.
As I stated earlier, it is the policy of the government as an employer that the compensation for its employees should neither leave nor trail that of similar occupations in the tax paying private sector.
Coincidentally, it is these same factors-skill, effort, responsibilities, and working conditions-which be analysed when comparing jobs within the Public Service to ensure that the principle of equal pay for work of equal value is being adhered to.
It should be pointed out that geographic location is not considered by the Canadian Human Rights Commission as a factor in determining whether wage discrimination is occurring.
In addition to comparing the rates of pay for public servants with those of their occupational counterparts in the private sector, the government as an employer must in accordance with the Canadian Human Rights Act, must also consider all the factors of employment, not just rates of pay.
