speechtext: The hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte had 10 minutes remaining for his speech, plus 10 minutes questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to continue my remarks on Bill C-44, particularly on the amendment put by the New Democratic Party.
When I spoke earlier, before debate on this bill was suspended, I dealt with each part of the amendment proposed by the New Democratic Party on Bill C-44, one after the other. I think it is illustrated quite clearly that none of the amendments being moved by the New Democratic Party to Bill C-44, upon serious, sober reflection, have any substance. The net effect of the amendments proposed by the new Democratic Party is, in essence, to suggest to the government and the people of Newfoundland that they have no role to play in the Hibernia development.
It represents an attitude on the part of the New Democratic Party that, in essence, big brother in Ottawa, as represented by the House of Commons, has to provide a degree of assurance in a whole variety of areas for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador because they are unable to provide for themselves any assurance about their future prosperity, the pace of development, the question of environmental protection, and, frankly, the question of equity participation by the federal government.
I think I was able to point out to my colleagues in the NDP, who I have to assume moved these amendments by accident and not by design, that, in fact, this motion is not well founded. It is my sincere hope that the New Democratic Party will withdraw these amendments and will not insist upon a vote on these amendments. Having heard something of the history of this development over the last decade or two, but in particular the last decade, for the New Democratic Party to insist upon these kinds of amendments in the House of Commons can only be seen as, first, an effort based upon an abysmal lack of knowledge about the history of the development. Second, it is essentially an attitude by the New Democratic Party-a paternalistic attitude at best-that says that the
Government Orders
people, and in particular the elected representatives in the government of Newfoundland and Labrador, are composed of people who have some kind of inferiority that prevents them from representing their own best interest and from participating in a full way as a partner in this development.
As a Newfoundlander, and one who has watched the 10 years of debate that have gone on, I cannot accept, no matter how well-intentioned, the paternalistic attitude of the New Democratic Party which says that Newfoundlanders are intrinsically incapable of seizing and seeing their own best interest and representing themselves; and that we, as members of Parliament from Edmonton East or elsewhere in the country, as well intentioned as we may be, really ought to look after those people of Newfoundland because they are not able to look after themselves.
I hope that it not the intention. In fact I have difficulty believing that is the intention of the New Democratic Party, and I would expect that members of that caucus upon reflection will withdraw these amendments which can only be considered by any rational, intelligent, informed, and engaged human being as, I hope unintended, insult and offence to the people and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador.
Clearly, it is unusual in the first instance for amendments to be moved on a bill even before that bill has gone to a legislative committee. That is rarely done in this place and, in essence, the attempt to move amendments becomes a form of filibuster. It becomes a basic vote of no confidence in the bill. They have not even given it a chance to be amended or studied in committee. They have not even heard witnesses and already they want to amend the bill.
I say to my colleagues in the New Democratic Party that, if they do not withdraw these amendments, no amount of woolly language and no amount of slippery words are going to convince Newfoundlanders of anything other than that the New Democratic Party of Canada, the national New Democratic Party, is opposed to the Hibernia development. The national New Democratic Party, as they say right in their amendment, does

not believe that Hibernia deserves the financial participation of the Government of Canada, and thereby of all Canadians, in this project on behalf of the notion of security of supply and, frankly, on behalf of the notion that Newfoundlanders deserve to share in the wealth and the opportunity for prosperity in the country.
My friend from Edmonton East, a member from Alberta, stood up and said: "I am from Alberta. I know all about energy development. It brings prosperity, but it brings problems too. It can bring disaster. It can bring misery. It can bring tremendous problems for the people who live in the province where energy development occurs." I found that an incredibly arrogant remark from the member.
I want to tell the member from Alberta, the member for Edmonton East, I know that energy development means challenge. I know and Newfoundlanders know that we have to be concerned about the pace of development. I know and Newfoundlanders know that we have to be concerned about protection of the environment, but let me tell him that the problems of prosperity are infinitely preferable to the problems of poverty. It is insulting and arrogant to suggest that he has suffered prosperity and that Newfoundlanders are far better off continuing to live in poverty.
It takes a special kind, may I suggest humbly, of pomposity to say: "I have had the wealth. We have rolled around in the prosperity of development and, believe you me, we have had difficulty from the vantage point of Alberta handling that prosperity, both the good and the bad. We want to keep you Newfoundlanders in your quaint little village with your high unemployment, with your particular culture, and with your particular way of life, shielded from the problems of prosperity, because you are really quaint, cute, valuable, and unique in your poverty." Well, I cannot accept that kind of reasoning from the New Democratic Party.
I have to believe that a couple of people ill-informed in that caucus, without the knowledge of the greater number of the members, hopefully without the knowledge of the leader and certainly without the knowledge of the New Democratic Party of Newfoundland and Labrador, moved this ill-considered amendment. Right now, as I speak the truth of the words that I utter on behalf of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, I
have to believe the confidence that I expressed in the ability of the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador to be a partner in this project and to participate with the national government and the consortium, and the confidence that I have that the legislature of Newfoundland will represent the views and interests of Newfoundland will permeate the fog that obviously prevails around the minds of those who drafted these amendments, Mr. Barrett and others, and the New Democratic Party will withdraw these amendments. The choices are two: Withdraw these amendments, recognize the ability of Newfoundland to speak for itself and to be a full partner; or have the courage to stand up and say clearly and without any equivocation that the New Democratic Party of Canada opposes Hibernia development.
The New Democratic Party of Canada is saying to Newfoundland that it does not believe, as a party, that the investment by the national government is warranted in Hibernia. It does not believe that the opportunity for new kinds of jobs, high-tech jobs, and permanent jobs should happen in Newfoundland and Labrador.
That is the challenge to the New Democratic Party. It is not to hide behind weasel words, not to hide behind phoney concern for Newfoundlanders, and not to assume that only the New Democratic Party can speak for Newfoundlanders, that they are unable to speak for themselves. The challenge is to admit honestly and openly that the party, the New Democratic Party, with these amendments, is saying to Newfoundland and Newfoundlanders everywhere: "You are not deserving. Hibernia is not deserving of the financial support of the federal government, and we oppose this project." Say it openly and say it honestly. At least it shall have the admiration of the people of my province for the courage of its convictions as much as we disagree. But do not hand us paternalism, do not hand us big brotherism, and do not tell us that they are doing it in our best interest because we, in our ignorance, know not what is good for us.
I say to the NDP: "Have the courage of your convictions, withdraw these foolish and insulting amendments, or stand clearly and say that you oppose the development of Newfoundland. Stand clearly and say that you genuinely believe that the so-called joy of poverty is preferable to the problems of prosperity. Say that to Newfoundlanders and they shall hold this New Demo-

cratic Party in judgment for this foolish delaying tactic of a project that is long overdue and urgently needed in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador."
Jack Whittaker (Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt):
Mr. Speaker, I listened very intently to the member's speech and I was astounded when he spoke of pomposity and arrogance because what I was hearing was exactly that. I heard a member who totally ignores, as perhaps governments in Newfoundland in the past have done, assistance or ideas from those outside.
I point the member to events in the have-not province of Saskatchewan under Tommy Douglas and the New Democratic Party. That was a party that knew where it wanted to go and how to get there. Unlike the Liberals and the Conservatives, this was a party with ideas, this was a party that was willing to come up with new ideas.
I ask the member, how many New Democratic Party governments has Newfoundland and Canada seen? Which parties have led the country and the provinces to the economic problems they have now? Which parties has it been?

Mr. Speaker, I was asked a question and I am glad to answer it. The member has asked how many New Democratic governments has Canada had. I am tempted to say in response to this so-called question that obviously we have had too many New Democratic Party governments in the country.
I am not one who usually spends much time having knee-jerk, philosophical reactions to the NDP. Frankly, on occasion, I find myself in agreement with it. But I must say that when I see this kind of bill I do not hesitate to tell my friends in the New Democratic Party that I think they have lost their minds. I do not think they have done their homework. I think they have been misled. I think they are confused. I think they do not even realize this is offensive.
The issue here is not that parties or people from other parts of Canada cannot give advice to Newfoundland. They are more than welcome to give advice to Newfoundland. They are more than welcome to come and visit my riding and give all the free advice they are willing to pass out. In many cases, it will be genuinely and happily accepted.
I do not subscribe to the notion that I am not able to speak about British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, Sas-

katchewan, or Manitoba. I think I am and I have an interest, as a Canadian member of parliament, in those provinces.
What I do subscribe to, as well as a right to speak about B.C., is a responsibility to understand what it is I am speaking about, a responsibility to have done my homework, a responsibility to understand the issue, a responsibility to understand the history of the development and an understanding to have knowledge not just biases or instincts as forces upon which I make my statements.
All I am saying to my hon. friends in the New Democratic Party-and they have not responded in detail-is that this amendment, moved even before we go into the legislative committee, the normal process, is a vote of non-confidence in Hibernia. I asked the member for Edmonton East earlier whether or not this meant that the bill should be defeated. He said that whether the amendment is passed or not, the bill ought to be defeated.
The member for Edmonton East had the courage to say that the New Democratic Party of Canada is opposed to Hibernia. In reality he said that, hidden behind this agenda of so-called amendments to help the quaint people of Newfoundland, is a clear statement by the New Democratic Party, the party of the little people, the party of the impoverished, the party of the poor, the party of the least advantaged, that it has given a boot to the people of Newfoundland, the province of highest unemployment in Canada.
Hidden behind the so-called party of energy self-sufficiency and security of supply is the party that says that offshore oil and gas ought not to be developed. That is what we have, hiding behind the party that has a member from Alberta who has prospered and seen some prosperity from energy development. It is the hypocrisy that the prosperity can be handled by those who live in Alberta, as difficult as it is, but Newfoundland really is better at handling poverty. They say we ought to stop this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would have hoped that the hon. member who represents a riding in Newfoundland would not take this debate to such a low.
The hon. member has succeeded in doing that. What is happening is that the hon. member for Edmonton East happens to come from Alberta-I am treading on dangerous ground and implying motives. What we are seeing now is a dynamic that is tearing our country apart. We are seeing it on a daily basis, and it is this kind of analysis that only feeds that dynamic.
The New Democratic Party represents all of Canada and works for the interests of all Canadians. The hon. member can very well cloak himself in the Newfoundland flag and feel that he is speaking for his riding. That is his right and duty. But we see things on a larger scale. We speak for all of Canada.
In fact, I think there are international aspects to this deal that need to be looked at, and I will address those in my speech. I just caution the member that the kind of regional hit-list that he is invoking today is not creative. It does not bring a solution to the problem. Because the hon. member who moved or supported the motion was from Edmonton East, it does not disqualify him from making comments on economic projects, on billions of dollars of taxpayers' dollars.
I ask the member this question. Does he believe that, because the hon. member for Edmonton East is from Alberta, it disqualifies him from commenting on this expenditure of Canadian taxpayer dollars?

Mr. Speaker, I made it very clear in my last comments that I would invite every hon. member of the New Democratic Party to come to Newfoundland to visit, to comment and to do some research to understand the history of the issue.
This hon. member has not been standing up and suggesting that hon. members outside Newfoundland have no right to comment, quite the contrary. In his last response, this hon. member made clear that he has a right and a responsibility to comment on issues affecting every other part of Canada. I frequently do in this place.
Along with the right to comment as a Canadian about Canadian issues, comes a responsibility to be informed.
Because I have a right to comment on what is happening in every part of Canada does not give me the right to comment without having done my homework. All I suggested to members of the New Democratic Party is not that they have no right to speak about Newfoundland issues, but that you have a responsibility to have done your homework. The issue I raise is not that members should not speak because they are from Alberta or British Columbia. What I have said is that the NDP should have done its homework on the issue.
Bill C-44 is a piece of enabling legislation which allows the federal government, the provincial government and a private sector consortium to reach arrangements for the development of Hibernia. However, the effect of the NDP amendments will eliminate the role of the government of Newfoundland and Labrador. The NDP are saying that there is only a role to be played by the federal government and the consortium.
The Minister of Energy is across from me now. The effect of these amendments is that the Newfoundland government has no role. There is a role for Ottawa. There is a role for the big boys in the corporate towers of Toronto but there is no role for Newfoundland. I cannot accept that. I am saying that if the NDP do not understand that is the effect of their amendment, perhaps it is by accident, not by design. It is one or the other. If you have not understood that is the effect of the amendment, Mr. Speaker, is what I am saying to my colleagues in the NDP, if it is an accident, withdraw the amendments and we will understand you made a mistake. If it is by design that you moved this kind of a motion, then have the courage to say it honestly and you will be judged accordingly by every region of Canada. This is not an issue about which you cannot speak. You have a right to speak. You have a responsibility to speak, but you have a responsibility as well to be informed. That is what I say to my colleagues in the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Speaker, it has been over 10 years since significant amounts of oil were discovered off the east coast of Canada. In that short time there has been a revolution in the energy sector in this country. Oil is not just oil anymore. How we find it and how we use it is still part of our energy policy, of course, but there is a new way of looking at energy policy. There is a new criterion by which energy
June 7, 1990

policy is to be judged. That new criterion is the effect the exploration, development and use of our energy resources have on the environment. After all, in the words of the Brundtland report, Our Common Future, "choosing an energy strategy inevitably means choosing an environmental strategy".
When it comes to the environment, this bill does not cut the mustard. In the absence of other concerted ameliorative actions, Bill C-44 proposes a course of action that is environmentally unsound. It promotes unsustainable development.
In my remarks this evening I would like first to address some of the serious environmental problems associated with offshore drilling and development. Second, I would like to take a broader view. I would like to consider how this bill fits into the government's sorry environmental record. What name comes to mind when you think of oil tankers plying our coastal waters? How about when I mention tankers running aground such as the Exxon Valdez. Oil tankers, waves, rocks and in the inevitable human error make a dangerous mix. Add fog, darkness, icebergs or screaming winds and tanker accidents, given time, become a virtual certainty.
Marine accidents do not just happen off the west coast. On October 9, 1984 a 30-thousand tonne Liberian-registered bulk carrier nearly rammed the drill rig Sedco 706 which had about 80 people on board. The ship came so close to the rig that it actually came between the anchor chain and the rig before being intercepted by supply vessel.
Canadians will also remember the tragic loss of life that occurred when the semi-submersible drill rig Ocean Ranger capsized and sank in 1982 during a furious storm. Busy tanker traffic to and from Hibernia's tanker loading facilities will inevitably increase the chances that just such an accident involving an oil tanker will occur. After the television coverage of the Exxon Valdez disaster, I do not have to remind Canadians of the environmental devastation that is caused by the thousands of tonnes of oil that can spew from a stricken tanker. I do not have to remind Canadians of the damage to fish stocks and to other marine life so fundamental to the lives of hundreds of thousands of Canadians in Atlantic Canada, people whose livelihoods are already threatened by actions of this Conservative government.
Government Orders
Oil spills also occur when offshore petroleum wells blow out. Since 1970 there have been six natural gas blowouts on the Canadian offshore, the most recent of which occurred in the Beaufort Sea just last June. In the Atlantic, three blowouts have occurred recently. On February 22, 1984, machine failure and lack of proper blowout prevention procedures caused a gas blowout of the semi-submersible drilling platform Vinland.
Another natural gas well blew out of control 290 kilometres off the Nova Scotia coast in February, 1985. That blowout lasted for several months. Yet another gas well blew out at West Venture, N-91, off Sable Island in April, 1985.
Natural gas well blowouts are more common and less harmful than oil well blowouts. But oil wells can blow too.
That is why I was shocked to learn that Canada is simply not prepared for an oil spill off the coast of Newfoundland. This fact is outlined in a report entitled Oil Spill Preparedness in the Upstream Petroleum Industry, released November 22,1989, by the Canadian Petroleum Association and the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada.
This report which was reviewed in the November 23, 1989 Financial Post, and again in the March 22, 1990, Globe and Mail, concluded that:
On the Grand Banks, industry does not presently have appropriate equipment or sufficient support vessels to respond immediately to an oil blowout and to clean up a blowout spill.
The report goes on to say that in a worst case scenario, as much as 32 times the volume of oil lost by the Exxon Valdez could be spilled into the most productive fishing grounds in the North Atlantic.
Moreover, the report states that in the event of a blowout during a storm on in the presence of significant amounts of ice:
- containment and recovery efficiency would be reduced, likely to zero per cent.
My colleague, the member for Edmonton East quizzed the president of the Canadian Petroleum Association, Mr. Maciej during a meeting of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources on February 8, 1990. Mr. Maciej said that:
-if the project proceeds it will be accompanied by the necessary preparedness to deal with oil spills.

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
When my colleague asked how this was to be guaranteed, Mr. Maciej replied: "It will just happen." He later elaborated slightly by saying that: "The approval of the department plan-requires that kind of action."
Well, most Canadians would not be very reassured by those comments. You can bet that my colleagues and I will be watching the situation very, very closely.
There is another significant threat to Hibernia and other similar projects that is not well known among Canadians who do not live in Atlantic Canada. Icebergs, huge icebergs towering like skyscrapers above the water, some weighing up to 50 million tonnes, are one of the most serious threats to east coast offshore activities.
Icebergs and bits that break off them are obviously a serious threat to tankers in the vicinity of Hibernia.
Drifting icebergs are also known to have forced personnel on movable drilling rigs to halt activities and flee their destructive presence.
Such icebergs are capable of gouging massive trenches in the sea bed, trenches up to 15 metres deep, 200 metres across and several kilometres long. This enormous power threatens Hibernia's proposed loading facilities and oil-gathering lines.
To be fair, this issue was considered during Mobile Oil's Environmental Impact Assessment in 1985. However, Cle Newhook then executive director of the Ocean Ranger Foundation, now leader of the Newfoundland and Labrador NDP, was quoted on October 17, 1985, in The Chronicle-Herald from Halifax expressing serious concerns that Mobile's assessment contained, in his words, "dangerous underestimates" of the wind, wave, current and ice conditions on the Grand Banks.
Many other people remain unconvinced that Hibernia's cement gravity-based structure, huge though it will be, together with its more fragile pipelines and tanker loading facilities will be capable of withstanding the full force of a massive iceberg during a raging storm.
It seems clear that many environmental questions about this project have not been answered, and indeed are difficult to answer definitively.
Oil industry analyst Ian Doig asked a crucial question in a Financial Post article on September 16, 1989, when he wrote:
The gravity based structure, GBS, will not just disappear when its use is finished. How do you hide 450,000 metric tons of concrete standing 357 feet tall?
Mr. Doig then suggested that, and I quote:
The revised project will probably have to be submitted to the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board (CNOPB) for approval. And certainly the plans for the eventual abandonment of the GBS structure will have to win environmental approval from Ottawa before work begins.
Speaking of environmental reviews, the Environmental Impact Statement conducted by Mobil and released in 1985 did not even consider or mention carbon dioxide emissions that will result from this fossil fuel megaproject. It is possible by aggressively pursuing the development of energy alternatives and energy conservation to ensure the Hibernia development would not result in an increase in Canada's CO2 emissions, even given the emission reduction target that we should be setting for ourselves in the next decade.
A major report released last August by the Toronto consulting group, DPA Group Incorporated, indicated that Canada could combat the greenhouse effect by slashing carbon dioxide emissions by 20 per cent by the year 2005 and save $100 billion in the process.
The point is that the government, through this bill, has effectively ignored the global warming issue altogether. I imagine some hon. members across the way are asking: What has carbon dioxide got to do with Bill C-44? It is simple. Bill C-44 provides for the extraction of a whole new source of CO2 emissions. Listen to what the Prime Minister said on June 27, 1988, at the International Conference on the Changing Atmosphere held in Toronto.
The world is coming to recognize what we believe to be self-evident-that development and environmental protection are mutually reinforcing, not mutually exclusive. Our economic activity must be increasingly compatible with today's environmental facts of life.
Later in the same speech, the Prime Minister stated:
In no area is the link between our economic activity and environmental disruption more evident or more troubling than in the area of energy policy. Canada is committed to applying the principles of sustainable development to our energy future.
June 7, 1990

So what about CO2 and global warming? The conference statement for the 1988 Toronto conference entitled The Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security stated that, and I quote:
The earth's atmosphere is being changed at an unprecedented rate by pollutants resulting from human activities, inefficient and wasteful fossil fuel use and the effects of rapid population growth in many regions.
It was stark language that the conference used in speaking of the changing atmosphere.
I want to draw the particular attention of the House to this quote:
Humanity is conducting an unintended, uncontrolled, globally pervasive experiment whose ultimate consequences could be second only to global nuclear war.
It should be noted that the Prime Minister did sign the Hague Declaration entitled Our Common Future: It's in our Hands. That declaration emphasized the importance of all countries doing their bit to prevent atmospheric pollution. It stated:
Because of the nature of the dangers involved, remedies to be sought involve-the duty of the community of nations, vis-a-vis future and present generations to do all that can be done to preserve the quality of the atmosphere.
More recently, before his untimely departure from cabinet, the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean made many statements about global warming on behalf of his government. He stated in a Toronto Star interview published on April 18, 1990 that:
We have sufficient indications (of global warming) to implement whatever action we can now.
On April 17, 1990 in Washington, D.C., speaking to reporters after a conference on global warming, the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean said that:
The price of inaction is too high to wait for further research.
In a column published in the November 1, 1989 edition of The Finance Post the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean wrote:
We can accept our responsibilities as leaders or we can abdicate.
Even the Energy Minister admits that actions need to be taken. He stated, during the December 11, 1989 meeting of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources, that:
Government Orders
Based on information I have received in the department from scientists and others who are working on global warming within the department, I am convinced that we have to reduce emissions, that they have negative effects on climate.
Clearly, on the level of government pronouncements, the Mulroney government is quick to agree that much needs to be done to protect the environment.
For its pronouncements to mean anything significant, Canada has to begin to put its own House in order. We clearly have a valuable role to play. After all, although Canada is directly responsible for about 2 per cent of the total global C02 emissions, we are one of the most energy-inefficient countries in the world. Canadians consume more energy per person than is the case in the U.S.A., Sweden, Germany, the U.K. and Japan, and the situation is getting worse.
From the perspective of energy use per thousand dollars GDP, we also use more energy than the U.S.A., Sweden, the U.K., Germany and Japan.
We live in a cold country, it is true, but in addition we are extremely wasteful. We could use substantially less energy, thereby polluting much less, without making significant changes to our way of life, but so far the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been heading in the opposite direction.
In the 1989-90 budget the government closed 12 conservation and renewable energy offices across the country. These offices provided information to people in the regions on how they could save money and energy at the same time. In fact they did not even interfere in the market-place, they only provided information, but the government closed them down. The government cut funding for conservation and renewable energy, according to figures from the Energy Department, from $410 million in 1984-85 to $40 million for 1990-91. That is a 90 per cent cut. This simply boggles the mind and it surely qualifies for yet another example of this government's stunning hypocrisy.
The Mulroney government publicly support the Brundtland Report and claimed to be very concerned about global warming. At the same time, it cut already limited funding for the most effective government programs to combat global warming and, instead, poured billions of dollars into Hibernia, a fossil fuel project that will add to global warming.

June 7, 1990
Government Orders
In conclusion, I urge the federal government to examine much more closely the environmental consequences of this project in particular, and its energy policy in general. This government has a long way to go to address environmental concerns.
The hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean is quoted as saying in The Globe and Mail report on April 19, 1990:
I don't think we should be afraid to be taking the lead.
Unfortunately, as this bill stands and in the absence of other concerted ameliorative actions, Bill C-44 proposes a course of action that is environmentally unsound and which constitutes unsustainable development.

Mr. Speaker, earlier today my New Democrat colleague, the member for Edmonton East, outlined why we in the New Democratic Party oppose this bill. Lie emphasized that we do not oppose the Elibernia project itself, but that we oppose this bill because it will not provide, among other things, the employment opportunities that the people of Newfoundland and Labrador deserve.
I do not propose to go into the sad history of dashed hopes and political opportunism that lies behind this bill, nor will I enter into a detailed description of the financial arrangements in the bill itself. Instead I will proceed directly from the remarks of my colleagues and focus on another serious shortcoming of the government's legislation.
This bill fails to provide adequate economic benefits for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador in particular, and for the people of Canada in general.
The Conservative government claims to support this bill, in part because of the economic spin-offs associated with the Hibernia development.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has repeatedly emphasized this point. For example, he was quoted in the Toronto Star on September 13, 1989, as saying:
We want the Hibernia project to take place. It is a project of
national importance and it is a project for regional benefits,
particularly for Newfoundland and Labrador.
In the House of Commons when my colleague from Edmonton East, the New Democratic energy critic, questioned the minister about plans the government
might have to minimize the project's environmental effects, the minister responded by claiming quite wrongly that we opposed economic development for Atlantic Canada. He stated and I quote:
New Democrats are opposed to Hibernia. I guess they want the unemployment in Newfoundland. They do not want the industrial benefits in Newfoundland. I am simply saying, you want all the benefits, but you do not want to take any of the responsibility.
I am pleased to say that the minister was totally wrong. We on this side of the House care very much about job creation, about everyday folk getting a fair deal, about our children having an even better opportunity in life than we have had.
That is why we examined the bill closely from the perspective of economic development. That examination demonstrated to us that the bill will not provide nearly enough benefit to Newfoundlanders and Canadians.
Contrary to the impression left by the minister that we imposed regional benefits, we want Newfoundlanders and Canadians to benefit from this project, and that is exactly why we oppose the bill. Just for a change, we want the federal government to take seriously the notion of economic diversification.
The simple fact is that the government, through this bill, is promoting a huge energy project that will bring precious little in the way of economic benefits to ordinary Newfoundlanders. That, to put it politely, is shameful.
The government should pay careful attention to the following statement contained in the background report prepared in 1986, written for the Royal Commission on Employment and Unemployment in Newfoundland and Labrador. It recognizes that Newfoundlanders will come up short in economic spin-offs. It states:
It is must be recognized that the majority of Hibernia development expenditures will be incurred outside Newfoundland. The skilled labour force in the province is limited. The number of local companies capable of significant involvement in the offshore industry is also relatively small.
Let me repeat that quotation from the Royal Commission on Employment and Unemployment in Newfoundland and Labrador.
It must be recognized that the majority of Hibernia development expenditures will be incurred outside Newfoundland.
June 7, 1990

Newfoundlanders will remember the two cabinet ministers holding a news conference in July 1988 to tell Quebecers that they could look forward to landing a large portion of the Hibernia contracts available to Canadian companies. At that time the Minister of Regional and Industrial Expansion estimated that Newfoundland would receive about $770 million worth of Hibernia contracts, while other provinces between them would get more than twice as much, about $1.83 billion in contracts. All that was before the free trade agreement and its national treatment provisions.
One of the original hopes of Hibernia was that it would provide Newfoundlanders with considerable economic benefit. This bill certainly will not satisfy that aspiration.
A study about how much money from offshore oil and gas exploration actually stays in Newfoundland was conducted by the offshore Business Development Division of the provincial Department of Development in 1985. That study found that in the preceding five years, while oil companies spent nearly $1.5 billion in Newfoundland, less than 20 per cent of that stayed in the province.
Newfoundlanders have also been led to expect that Hibernia will bring royalty and tax money into the province. Incredibly, Newfoundlanders will gain much less than they thought they would just a few years ago.
Last year the official in charge of Norway's multi-billion dollar petroleum industry was quoted in the St. John's Evening Telegram of March 11, 1989 calling the Hibernia deal "more generous to the oil companies" than would be allowed in his country.
In fact, even before the recent redesign of the project which will result in fewer benefits accruing to Newfoundland, the Hibernia deal was severely criticized for being a very bad deal for Atlantic Canada.
For its part the provincial government has given up an enormous amount in potential benefits by granting a sales tax holiday, providing corporate income tax concessions and designing a royalty regime that will result in the province forgoing billions of dollars on royalties. Many observers have pointed out that the provincial government made so many concessions, and Newfoundlanders will benefit so little from the project.
Government Orders
The people of Newfoundland and Labrador deserve more than this. Yet the Conservative government insists that Newfoundlanders should be grateful and they want us to support this bill, this financial strait-jacket for Newfoundland and Labrador.
We New Democrats are not the only ones to recognize that the Hibernia deal is not a good one for Atlantic Canada. A former federal Liberal energy critic indicated that a much better deal could have been struck. While in opposition the present Premier of Newfoundland was a vocal opponent of the deal. Mr. Wells' opposition is rather more muted these days, but he certainly was strongly opposed to the deal at an earlier stage when he was in opposition. It was instructive to remember what Mr. Wells was saying a few months ago. He said:
Mr. Peckford and the federal government did a terrible job on the Hibernia deal. The agreement in principle gives away more than we are getting in return. There are no significant benefits for Newfoundland.
He also said:
Unless there is a massive increase in the price of oil, which nobody at this stage is predicting, there will be very low royalties to start with, and the royalties that are paid will result in virtually a dollar for dollar reduction in (federal) equalization payments. So the net cash value to Newfoundland will be virtually nil.
The problems with the deal do not end with the provincial royalty and tax regime. What about the economic spin-offs? What about the opportunities for business in Newfoundland to supply goods and services for the project?
They do not look good. Based on the offshore oil experience in Norway and Scotland, Newfoundland's development minister is already warning local companies that they might have a hard time meeting the exacting standards the owners of the project will demand. He said: "Alarm bells should be going off in company heads right now".
The article from which I just quoted went on to refer to what he called a typical purchase order of Mobil Oil and said:
The quality control requirements imposed by the offshore oil industry are more stringent than those normally encountered by Canadian contractors and suppliers, excepting perhaps those involved in the nuclear industry.

Government Orders
That sounds a lot like a foreign multinational letting Newfoundland business know that it is going to be out of luck. But there is more: perhaps the government will help local businesses meet those exacting standards imposed by the oil industry.
According to one article, about $500,000 has already been spent on this, but according to the province's energy minister right now only three or four businesses meet the specifications for quality control. Three or four businesses only, Mr. Speaker, and according to the minister only a number of others will be able to meet those standards. That is clearly not economic diversification.
What about using the old to diversify the Newfoundland economy? There will be no luck there either.
In Alberta, petroleum feed stocks were provided to the petrochemical industiy at a reduced price to give it a competitive advantage. The trade deal prevents Newfoundland from enjoying this diversification tool. The deal prohibits government policies intended to result in energy prices for domestic purposes that are lower than export prices. It is practically impossible for Newfoundland to spur local refining or develop a profitable petrochemical industry using oil stock from the Hibernia and nearby fields.
Similarly under the trade deal there is no possibility that Newfoundlanders in particular, or Canadians in general, will have priority access to Hibernia oil subsidized with Canadian public funds.
What seems more likely is that most of the Hibernia oil will be shipped straight to the United States, and that most of it will not even be refined in Newfoundland.
Not only will Newfoundlanders not get the jobs that refining represents, not only will the province not get the economic spin-offs that could come from refining it, on top of it all Canadians by subsidizing Hibernia will in effect be subsidizing American consumers.
That is not what we in the New Democratic Party call economic diversification for Newfoundlanders.
Aside from these forgone financial opportunities, there are also very real social costs associated with any megaproject like Hibernia. These often receive veiy little attention, even though large energy developments in other provinces have all too frequently led to serious
social problems resulting from rapid population shifts, inadequate planning, and a lack of human services and facilities.
The Community Services Council recommended to the Hibernia environmental assessment panel that Mobile should be required to set aside adequate funding for social planning and research. The Canadian Mental Health Association indicated that not enough base line data existed to forecast accurately the social services that will be required.
Other organizations have stressed the need for additional day care facilities in the province so that women are not prevented from obtaining those employment opportunities that will exist.
All these things take planning. All these things will end up costing the people of Canada and Newfoundland money.
Given these often ignored costs and given the deal's shocking paucity of benefits for Newfoundland, it is not surprising that even the Premier of Newfoundland stated in a state of the province address on January 11 the following:
It may well be in the best interests of the people of this province to
leave the oil in the ground until we get the real benefits.
Whenever I think about this bill and the agreement behind it and about all those people who believe that it makes no economic sense for the people of province or the country, I am reminded of the great myth that Conservatives are supposed to be good economic managers. I think this is a good example of hypocrisy on the part of the government.
On the one hand the Conservatives frequently portray themselves as good economic managers and foster the ideology of the market oriented approach. Yet here they are using billions of dollars of public funds and a massive intervention in the market-place to subsidize a project that makes little economic sense and will bring few benefits to Newfoundlanders. This point is not lost on business commentators. Oil analyst, Ian Doig, points out that of all oil production in the world 99.5 per cent of it would be less costly than Hibernia oil. The Associate Editor of The Financial Post, Terence Corcoran, in an article on July 26, 1988 wrote:
At best, Hibernia and the other megadollar sinkholes re-establish corporations as corporate welfare bums-
June 7, 1990

Quite clearly, the Conservative market ideology demands that ordinary Canadians survive as best they can in the market-place. The wealthy and the powerful, however, apparently have to be induced to venture into those inhospitable climes.
And what an inducement Hibernia backers will get: up to more than $3 billion in free money, loans, and loan guarantees. Of that, more than $1 billion will be in the form of a direct grant, free money with no strings attached. A billion dollars in free government money can be a wonderfully comforting thing to have when the chill winds of the market start to blow.
Not even the Alberta government, which for years was rolling in petro-dollars, was ever that profligate. When the time came for it to ante up its contribution to the giant Syncrude oil sands plant in Fort McMurray, the Alberta government made sure that Albertans could share in the project's successes. Through a combination of equity and convertible debentures later converted to equity, the Alberta government came to hold 16.74 per cent of Syncrude directly. The 16.74 per cent share generated returns for the people of Alberta of more than $410 million in the 1980s alone. That is almost twice the original cost to Alberta of its participation in the project.
By investing in Syncrude through equity and convertible debentures instead of simply giving away money as this government is doing, the people of Alberta secured a tidy profit over time and have retained share holdings which have doubled in value over the years going from about $250 million to over $500 million. What is more, the $500 million is still there to be used in any future projects the government might desire.
The question which hangs on this bill is: Why not equity? Why did the Conservative government not obtain an equity participation in the Hibernia project? Why not secure for the Canadian people a dollar's worth of equity for every dollar they put into the project? Surely, if the Conservative Government of Alberta is capable of realizing and acting upon this sensible concept, the Conservative Government of Canada should take the hint, but no it prefers the role of corporate Santa Claus,
Government Orders
giving billions of dollars away, to the role of prudent husbander of the public purse.
In summary, this bill fails to provide for adequate economic benefits for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador in particular and for the people of Canada in general. That has been pointed out by many in Newfoundland, including the present Premier of Newfoundland. For this reason alone, as well as for the other reasons presented by my colleagues, the bill deserves defeat at second reading.
For those reasons, I support the amendments of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca.

June 7, 1990
Adjournment Debate

Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, tonight I would like to return to a question I raised in the House on May 25, 1990 to which the leader of the government in the House of Commons responded on behalf of the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. The question concerned in a narrow sense the Scotia Synfuels Project for coal liquefaction in Cape Breton and specifically the approval by the government of an application by the company for a package of assistance containing principally the Cape Breton Investment Tax Credit and certain loan guarantees available through the department of Industry, Science and Technology.
The Scotia Synfuels Project in its proposal to use a liquefaction process to convert high sulphur Cape Breton coal in an oil mixture into a clean source of energy to serve the needs of Atlantic Canadians and for export has been under development for several years. The technology has been proven.
The jobs and the spin-off benefits in eastern Nova Scotia are well established. As well, the general soundness of the project in environmental and other terms are widely acknowledged and well established. They were enumerated at some length in a speech in this House by my colleague, the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys on May 28.
While the question concerned the narrow issue of the government's support for this project, it concerns broader issues as well. It concerns the seriousness of this government's commitment to seeking out more environmentally friendly ways of producing energy sources from our fossil fuels. It concerns the seriousness of the government's commitment to ensuring that Canada is on the leading edge of technology in an area in which we should have an important comparative advantage and
which is definitely going to be vital for the future success of our economy. It concerns as well the seriousness of this government's commitment to fostering industrial development in Atlantic Canada. It concerns the willingness of this government to take risks, even moderate risks, in support of progressive technology in a part of the country that badly needs it.
In his reply to my colleague's remarks on May 28 the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration pointed out that his government had funded to the tune of 50 per cent the cost of a feasibility study on this project. He also said that "this government wants to be certain that an investment of public funds results in durable and viable jobs for the long term".
The principals of this project are anxious to do whatever they can to prove to this government and to demonstrate the technical and commercial viability of this project. They have been doing so for several years. They have had Wood Gundy, one of the prominent investment firms in Canada, produce a study which declared the project commercially viable, provided that the regular incentive programs available through this government were made available to the project, including the Cape Breton Investment Tax Credit. They have responded to the concerns raised by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources about the economics of the project and have proven that the economics of the project are indeed favourable because and not in spite of its location in the east coast of Canada.
The principals are anxious to proceed with the next stage of the project, to firm up the cost estimates, to establish the market sources for the product, and to secure the necessary financing so that construction and jobs can commence.
The people of Cape Breton, and in particular the people of the Strait of Canso area where industrial activity has lagged since this government came to power in 1984, are anxious to see this project proceed. They are anxious to see the benefits and the jobs which will come through the commencement of this important project, but the government keeps waffling. It keeps passing the buck from one department to the other, from Energy, Mines and Resources to DIST, from DIST to ACOA, and from ACOA back to Energy, Mines and Resources.
June 7, 1990

The company is frustrated. It wants to know what more it can do. What other information can it provide this government? What concrete conditions does it need to meet in order to be able to get a firm, positive answer on the part of this government as to whether it will be able to receive this investment tax credit which is vital to the success of this project? What is more aggravating is that the government does not really need to share the risk upfront on this project. The investment tax credit will only cost the government money once the company has developed investment sources and the project has begun to earn taxable revenue. The project could earn up to $800 million in tax revenue for the government during its life, not to mention some of the other benefits.
Although there are some risks in the loan guarantees and other incentives that the government would have to provide, they pale in comparison to the opportunity of developing an economically depressed region in Canada with a leading, environmentally efficient process for coal and oil liquefaction, a project which is Canadian owned and which will use our local coal resources in a cleaner, superior way which can lead to lower acid rain emissions and which can be a show-piece to Canada's future environmental agenda.
This government's failure to support fully the Scotia's Synfuels initiative is incomprehensible and amazingly short-sighted. The U.S. government is not so short sighted. It has already indicated through the Department of Energy its support for a similar project in Ohio. It has urged this government to support that project.
We have our own project in Cape Breton. Why does the government insist on demanding additional information from a company which has been so co-operative in the past? Why does the government not simply approve this project, take a risk on Atlantic Canada and allow these jobs to commence.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much agree with the hon. member when he says that the Scotia Synfuels proposal in Cape Breton has considerable potential to economically benefit eastern Nova Scotia.
I would like at this time to reiterate some of the points which the minister responsible for ACOA made last week in this Chamber. Certainly the Government of Canada has been tiying to enhance economic opportuni-
Adjoumment Debate
ties in the Atlantic region by considering every alternative employment opportunity that will help to diversify the economy. I would suggest that the very creation of ACOA has been a step forward in that regard.
It must be pointed out, however, that while the hon. member has again pressed for the approval of investment tax credit for the Synfuels project, it is really Industry, Science and Technology, as the hon. member knows, rather than ACOA which has the lead role for the federal government on this project.
ACOA, as the development agency for small to medium sized businesses can, of course, and will play an advocacy role.
That being said, I wish to point out that federal officials have devoted a great deal of time to looking at the long term economic viability of this project, and its potential to create long term employment.
I wish to point out, as the hon. member has already indicated, that the federal government did help fund 50 per cent of the costs of a technical feasibility study to which he referred, at a very significant sum of some $650,000. That study, of course, was completed in November of 1989.
As has often been the case in the past, I speak of prior to 1984 when governments were interested in establishing projects in order to produce a quick fix, this government wants to be certain that any investment of public funds results in durable and viable jobs for the long term.
With respect to Scotia Synfuels, ACOA and Industry, Science and Technology officials want to be sure, and I think most Canadians would understand why this is so, that this project valued at well over $400 million is sufficiently viable to justify the substantial expenditure of public funds which would be required from Investment Tax Credit.
While a number of jobs this facility promised to create is certainly impressive, there is still more study required before any decision can be made.

Mr. Speaker, almost a month ago, I had a question for the Prime Minister concerning the people of the riding of Lauri-er-Sainte-Marie. In my question I asked the Prime Minister when the government was going to provide

June 7, 1990
Adjournment Debate
economic measures to help the residents of Laurier- Sainte-Marie. I was not satisfied with the Prime Minister's answer, and that is why I am asking the same question today, although I will be more specific. When will the government take economic steps to help the people of Laurier-Sainte-Marie?
I would like to explain that the unemployment rate in this riding is almost 20 per cent. At a time when direct government assistance is needed to help these people, it would seem the government is doing the exact opposite.
I will mention some of the economic measures that have had a disastrous impact on the people of Laurier- Sainte-Marie.
First of all, there is the GST, the Goods and Services Tax that will soon come into force. It will be a heavy burden for people who are in no position to pay this kind of tax, any more than other Canadians.
Second, a federal Budget has just been adopted, obliging the provinces to take over an increasingly larger share of the responsibility for various social programs. I will name some of the programs that are vital to Laurier-Sainte-Marie-medical care for the elderly, for instance. Federal budget cuts are going to affect medical care for senior citizens. Even the Government of Quebec has condemned the cuts affecting these people.
Third, this Budget is a blow to students who need federal assistance for postsecondary education. This budget will not provide the assistance we received in the past.
Furthermore, we also have a problem with the unemployment insurance reform legislation. The people in Southeast Montreal need the safety net. They need the unemployment insurance they have been paying for for years. Unfortunately, the so-called reform adopted by the federal government-I wonder whether this is not misleading advertising, because the reform gives less to these people. Instead of protecting them, it provides less protection than they received in the past.
That is why the Churches, unions, charitable organizations, local citizens groups and others objected to this so-called unemployment insurance reform. I deplore the
fact that after all the work done by Jean-Claude Malepart, who was very much a populist, to protect his people-and I think we in this House must recognize one thing, and I believe everyone will agree, Conservatives as well as Liberals, that Jean-Claude Malepart, the former Liberal member, did a terrific job of representing his constituents- not just Liberal voters but all his constituents. This was a guy who worked for the poor-people who are vulnerable, people who have no hope. He did a good job. And now, for more than six and a half months, these people have lacked representation in Parliament. And instead of providing tax measures to help these people, the government does the exact opposite.
What I would like the government to do is implement three things: first of all, measures to provide subsidies under the Employment and Immigration Act, through Challenge 90; second, provide grants for job development programs, and I am sure it would be a great help to the people of Laurier-Sainte-Marie; and finally, drop this unemployment insurance legislation, because it will make matters even worse for the people of Laurier- Sainte-Marie. This time I expect a reply, and I hope it will be a clear and sensible reply, one that will give genuine consideration to the needs of the people in the riding of Laurier-Sainte-Marie.

Mr. Speaker, on May 3 of this year I rose in my place to put a question to the Minister responsible for Canada Post because I had just learned that 92 Canadian communities were going to lose mail-sorting operations and jobs within their communities.
One of those 92 communities is my own home city of North Battleford, Saskatchewan, a city and an operation that I know quite well. Canada Post announced on May 2 that they were going to increase efficiencies. I put quotation marks around that word "efficiencies" because that is the word that they use, but which is yet to be really defined in terms of Canada Post. Canada Post said it would increase efficiencies by streamlining the mail sorting process. The whole thing is to take effect on September 1 of this year.
What are these efficiencies that they are talking about? They are going to put a second mail collection box on street comers where ones already exist. These twin boxes, as they call them, will allow the postal user to deposit mail for local delivery in one box and mail for out-of-town delivery in another box. What on the surface seems very simple is otherwise crazy. In implementing this twin box policy, Canada Post will reduce the number of street box locations where mail can be deposited and across Canada reduce its work-force of inside sorters by 800 to 1,000 persons.
In North Battleford they eliminated positions that equal six full-time and two part-time, a situation the postal workers estimate in the city of North Battleford alone to be as much as $300,000 a year. There is no reason for this loss to these workers, their families, to our communities, and the disruption is as great on the service where the so-called simplification situation will actually lead to more handling of the mail.
Let us use the example of the mail going from North Battleford to Lloydminster now. This mail is now sorted in my home town of North Battleford. It is put on a truck in North Battleford and brought to Lloydminster where it is delivered. It is a very simple process.
Under the new system, after September 1, the mail will now be deposited in these out-of-town mail boxes in North Battleford. It will be trucked east to Saskatoon for sorting and then trucked west again through the city of
Adjournment Debate
North Battleford on to Lloydminster. The extra handling will result in slower mail and likely more losses. There are no efficiencies here.
Other small communities around the city of North Battleford will be effected in exactly the same way. Today, mail going to Maymont just a few miles outside of North Battleford to the east, is sorted and sent for delivery to Maymont, but after September 1 that mail from North Battleford to Maymont will first go through Maymont to Saskatoon for sorting, back through Maymont to North Battleford for putting on the contractor's delivery truck and then back to Maymont. That mail which previously took about 40 minutes to get delivered will now pass through Maymont three times before it gets to its destination. The more handling there is the greater the incidents of error.
Let me give one other situation concerning the town of Meadow Lake. Meadow Lake is north of the city of North Battleford. Mail posted before midnight in North Battleford today will arrive in Meadow Lake the next day. In September that mail posted in North Battleford will first go to Saskatoon in the south, then back through North Battleford to arrive in Meadow Lake. Unless mail is posted before 4.30 in the afternoon, it is guaranteed to take an extra day for delivery between North Battleford and Meadow Lake, just a short 100 mile distance. The service has obviously been reduced to these communities as a result of the new efficiencies introduced by Canada Post.
Let us not forget one other situation. If you are mailing locally, and you happen to make a mistake and your mail goes into the wrong box, your mail from North Battleford now goes to Saskatoon, whether you want it to or not.
Therefore, since this rationalization is not more efficient, it can only be for one other purpose, to get a reduced workforce, lower costs and a greater chance to increase the profile of the corporation. In this way, the government can sell it to the private sector as recommended by a government committee.
There is no justification for a privatized post office which would never provide service to rural Canada adequately. The Crown corporation exists to meet certain communication needs for Canadians and only a Crown corporation accountable to Canadians through Parliament will meet those needs.

June 7, 1990
Adjournment Debate
On May 3, I called this latest move by Canada Post a stupid idea and I called on the minister to maintain the Crown corporation and establish a full-time postal commission to return accountability to the post office and give Canadians some control over the type of service they deserve.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post's network rationalization program is another step in the corporation's efforts to optimize the use of both mechanized sorting equipment and better transportation links.
Once the program is implemented, as it has been in a number of communities already, mail will be streamlined into mechanized plants for maximum efficiency and faster sortation and distribution. Some delivery improvements will be achieved, particularly forward mail, and in all cases the corporation will maintain its present delivery standards. The program allows for the elimination of one step from the existing mail processing operation.
Through the twin-letter box system, local mail will continue to be sorted by the local post office in most cases, while mail destined for other locations will be moved immediately to the nearest mechanized facility for speedier handling. Similar changes have already been successfully implemented in other communities.
The changes undertaken with the network rationalization program are proven methods of increasing efficiency, while at the same time improving service.
So I ask, why is the hon. member so opposed to this positive accomplishment, when the corporation has already stated that no one, and I repeat, no one will lose their employment because of this, and all affected employees will be dealt with in accordance with their respective collective agreements. The allegations that this program will cost jobs, as some have alleged, of close to 1,000 postal workers is clearly based on erroneous information.
